entries.authors: Kesarwani M, Channarayapatna S, Paul D, Goswami V

entries.tried: Carbon, oxygen and strontium isotopes in cattle/buffalo tooth enamel (from the title).

entries.title: Modelling the possible archaeological past(s): Agent-based modelling of Harappan seal use and survival
entries.question: Why are Harappan sealings so rare if seals were used to make impressions?
entries.tried: Agent-based model (NetLogo) of seal, sealing and house production and decay at Mohenjo-daro DK-G South.
entries.method_data: DK-G South: about 490 seals and 10 sealings from over 20 feet of deposit (more than 15% of all Harappan seals). Corpus-wide about 2200 seals vs about 250 impressions. Four scenarios, seal-energy 3 or 10 impressions per seal, 50 iterations.
entries.key_results: If each seal made at least 50 impressions, about 110,000 sealings would have existed; the ~250 known are 0.227% of that. In the models, survival leaves about 22-24 seals but hundreds to over 1,000 sealings, far more sealings than found.
entries.limits: Early-stage model; parameters are guesses; house counts become unrealistic (e.g. 1702) in one scenario. Does not model excavation recovery bias in detail.
entries.ideas_for_us: Directly relevant to administration framing. The seal-to-sealing ratio (about 2200 : 250) argues against a Mesopotamian-style sealing bureaucracy. Use object type (seal vs sealing vs tablet) as a covariate and test whether sign sequences on sealings are a non-random subset of seal texts.

entries.title: Indus masked-sign restoration: code, splits and predictions
entries.question: A team released code, data and predictions for a model that guesses damaged or missing signs.
entries.tried: The team rebuilt a corpus from Mahadevan 1977 by cutting sign crops from a scan of the book, proposing a sign number for each crop with an image matcher, and approving every sign by hand.
entries.method_data: They kept only single-line texts with no lost or doubtful sign and removed exact repeats, following the EBUDS rules of Yadav et al. 2009 without the direction filter. They split the texts into five folds by a hash of the object number, so all sides of one object fall in the same fold, and used fold 0 as the test set. They masked every position of every test text in turn and asked three models to guess the missing sign: a Kneser-Ney trigram (KN-3), a five-seed transformer, and a blend of the two. They also ranked candidate restorations for 360 damaged texts that have exactly one lost sign (Table S11). The deposit holds folds, masked positions, model probabilities and Table S11, but not the corpus or the true signs, because the book is not theirs to redistribute.
entries.key_results: The rebuilt corpus has 1,585 texts, 7,105 signs and 373 distinct signs; train, validation and test hold 1,161, 121 and 303 texts (REBUILD.md, step 6). Of 3,753 inscribed sides, 3,297 are single-line, 2,626 have no lost passage, 2,398 have no doubtful sign, and 1,585 remain after removing repeated texts (REBUILD.md, step 6 table). On all 1,403 masked test positions, Hit@1 is 39.56% for KN-3, 37.49% for the transformer and 40.84% for the blend; Hit@5 is 60.23%, 58.23% and 62.01% (README.md, 'Checking a rebuild'). The blend weight on KN-3 is 0.45, chosen on validation texts (README.md, 'Predictions'). Table S11 covers 360 damaged texts: 170 initial, 179 terminal and 11 medial gaps, and 111 of them have an intact parallel elsewhere in the corpus (README.md, 'Table S11'). None of the 7,105 corpus signs was approved by the automatic rule; every sign was verified by a person (REBUILD.md, step 5). The authors warn that where a model is confident its top guess is often the attested sign, so the predictions are not independent of the texts they were made for (README.md, 'Predictions'). Our own bench of this deposit found that 107 of the 296 scored test texts (36%) have a near-copy in training, and on clean texts the transformer gets 28.5% Hit@1 against 29.8% for a plain trigram. Retraining their own code without those near-copies lowers every model by about 6-7 points of Hit@1 against a size-matched control; the transformer still does not beat their KN-3 (experiments/bench_restoration/RESULTS.md).
entries.limits: The deposit is unusually careful: hash-based folds, a written rebuild procedure, a script that checks a rebuild, and a self-audit for leaked sign data. Their own numbers already show the simple trigram matching or beating the transformer, which they report rather than hide. Folds are hashed by object, not by text family, so near-copies of one formula sit on both sides of the split and inflate every model's score. Only exact repeats were removed; texts one sign apart, or contained in a longer text, stay in, which is where the leakage comes from. Because the corpus and true signs are withheld, nobody can check the scores without first re-reading the whole book by hand.
entries.ideas_for_us: We graded it, then retrained their own code. 36% of its test texts have a near-copy (one sign off, or contained) in its training texts. Training without those near-copies lowers every model's first-guess accuracy by about 6-7 points, compared with dropping the same number of unrelated texts. Without them, the neural model still does no better than their simple three-sign model. Score the Table S11 restorations against a second witness: for each damaged M77 text, look up the same object in ICIT and check whether ICIT reads the lost sign, then ask where that sign falls in the blend's ranking. (This is the only ground truth for real damage, as opposed to artificial masking, and texts with no parallel show whether restoration works where it matters.) Calibrate the 'context beyond three signs adds nothing' finding: train the same transformer and trigram on planted language texts and on SIGIL texts cut to Indus length, with family-clean splits, and see whether the transformer beats the trigram there. (If a transformer gains on short language texts but not on Indus or SIGIL, the null gain on Indus says something about long-range structure; if it gains nowhere, the null result is only a short-text effect.)
entries.read_note: partial (the Zenodo record metadata and the full deposit README.md and REBUILD.md, plus the project's own bench of the deposit; the accompanying paper itself was not found online, so its text, tables and discussion were not read)

entries.title: A Computational Evaluation of Syllabic Hypotheses for Rongorongo: Evidence from N-gram Analysis
entries.question: Can Rongorongo be read as a one-sign-one-syllable substitution of Rapa Nui, and how well does a frequency-based attack work on known Rapa Nui text of tablet length?
entries.tried: Calibrate a genetic-algorithm substitution attack on enciphered Rapa Nui text first, then apply it to two Rongorongo transliterations.
entries.method_data: Five Rapa Nui sub-corpora (each over 10,000 words; Manuscript E, Campbell songs, Englert, a textbook, Gospel of Matthew). 1000-syllable fragments enciphered with a random key. Fitness from unigram/bigram/trigram counts plus rank penalties; GA in two phases (top 20 signs, then top 50). Every text x model-corpus pair is crossed, plus a pooled model.
entries.key_results: With the model built from the same sub-corpus, about 26 syllables are recovered on average and over 80% of the text is covered. With a model from a different genre of the same language, the average falls to 10 syllables and 37% coverage; the worst pair (Manuscript E text, Matthew model) gives 4.6 syllables. A pooled model of all five corpora gives 17 syllables and 62% coverage. Fitness correlates with accuracy at 0.75; below 2,500,000 points a solution is treated as noise. CEIPP Rongorongo scores 1.0M-1.3M (below the noise threshold); the rongopy transliteration scores 2.0M-2.7M (gray zone).
entries.limits: Single GA with hand-set bonuses, not a likelihood. One fragment length only (1000 signs). Pair-level means only; no replicate spread reported. Genre mismatch is not quantified as a divergence.
entries.ideas_for_us: Add a full text-genre x model-genre cross table at fixed size as a planted mismatch ladder inside one language. Measure each cell's excess cross-entropy and check that it falls on the same boundary as the cross-language pairs. Test a pooled multi-genre model as a cheap way to cut mismatch. Their score-to-accuracy calibration (noise threshold) is a model for turning our attack score into a solvability flag on Indus.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Should change the plan: the 'same language across genres' pair is not a near-zero-mismatch control, since genre mismatch alone cut recovery by more than half at 1000 signs. Measure its excess cross-entropy and treat it as a real mismatch point, not as a lambda=1 stand-in.

entries.title: On the Non-Specificity of Statistical Measures Used in Script Decipherment (SIGIL)
entries.question: If a made-up emblem system matches every statistic, statistics alone cannot prove the signs are writing.
entries.tried: The author built SIGIL, a generator of seal-like inscriptions for a made-up administrative world, where every text has a stored meaning but no sign has a sound.
entries.method_data: Texts are assembled from optional opener, dedication, office, ledger and terminal blocks, with urn processes giving a few frequent and many rare signs, licensed deity-epithet pairs, tally marks, ligatures and a trading outpost. Before scoring, he closed a registry of 54 published methods and scored exactly only those whose Indus result and decision rule he could reproduce. He also rebuilt the wider battery of entropy, Zipf, positional, prediction, restoration, classifier and network measures. He ran a dictionary-matching decipherment engine on SIGIL to read it as English, Sanskrit and Tamil, with grouped held-out tests and random-key controls.
entries.key_results: The canonical corpus has 3,000 core texts, 13,717 tokens, 419 attested core types and a mean length of 4.572 signs (Table 1, p. 4). SIGIL gets the same category as Indus on all six exactly scored outcomes; for example the repetition ratio is 0.646 for SIGIL and 0.575 for Indus, both on the non-linguistic side of 0.10 (Table 2, section 6.1). Its Zipf-Mandelbrot exponent is 2.574 against the published EBUDS value of 2.59 (section 6.2, Figure 2). 39 SIGIL signs cover 80% of text-initial tokens and 10 cover 80% of final tokens, paralleling 82 against 23 for Indus (section 6.2, Figure 5). The Lee classifier calls SIGIL 'writing: syllables' in all 27 sensitivity settings (section 6.2). Restoration puts the true sign inside the 90% candidate set in 84.88% of 275,300 trials, against a published Indus figure of 74% (section 6.2). Dictionary coverage of SIGIL reaches 83.0% for English, 88.13% for Sanskrit and 67.73% for Tamil in sample, against random-key means of 6.50%, 5.77% and 9.48% (section 6.3). Six bootstrap Sanskrit-script keys agree on only 9.30% of sign values although each parses over 93.5% of the corpus (section 6.3).
entries.limits: A single explicit non-language that passes the tests is enough to show those tests are not sufficient for language, and the registry and public generator make this checkable. The paper is careful to claim only existence: it gives no likelihood ratio and no estimate of how common such systems are. SIGIL was built with the published statistics in view and is not a held-out sample, so it shows compatibility, not that emblem systems usually look like this. Only six dependent outcomes from three method families are in the exact score; the other 48 methods are reconstructions or excluded. The fictional setting is not a model of Harappan society.
entries.ideas_for_us: Every new claim we test must also fail on SIGIL-style emblem data. We use it as a standing negative control. Make bootstrap key agreement a gate for any reopened phonetic key: refit the key on resampled texts and require value agreement well above SIGIL's 9.30%. (Coverage alone is reached on a corpus that encodes nothing; stability of values across resamples is something SIGIL fails and a real key should pass.) Use SIGIL's outpost as the control for our Gulf round-seal result: compare the bits-per-sign penalty of the Gulf seals under a core-trained model with the penalty SIGIL's outpost texts get under a SIGIL core model. (SIGIL's outpost scores near zero likelihood purely from regional emblem events, so a Gulf 'foreign dialect' reading must exceed what an emblem system already produces.)

entries.title: A Glyph Is Not a Letter, a Token Is Not a Word, a Space Is Not a Space: What the Units of Voynichese Are Not
entries.question: Are Voynich glyphs letters, tokens words, and blanks word spaces, and does a calibrated substitution attack find any plaintext language?
entries.tried: Learn multi-glyph units (BPE, then Brown-style class merging), run a class-to-letter substitution attack against several language models, and calibrate it on synthetic homophonic ciphers of Latin against both the right and a wrong language model, with a fitted order-3 surrogate as a matched null.
entries.method_data: Zandbergen-Landini transliteration; matched prose, cipher and pseudo-text controls; quire-level resampling. Language models for Latin, vowelless Latin, Italian, German, French, English and consonantal Hebrew. Five synthetic cipher configurations x five seeds; eight restarts per mapping search.
entries.key_results: On the synthetic Latin ciphers the pipeline recovers 73.7-92.6% of the frequency-weighted mapping with the right language, against 0-23.4% for the wrong-language mapping. The real-minus-surrogate language-match differential is positive in all 25 right-language runs (configuration means +0.13 to +0.52) and +0.05 to +0.13 against a wrong-language (German) model. Voynich gives -0.154 to +0.075 (mean -0.0085), at or below the wrong-language band. Glyph conditional entropy is 2.7 bits against about 3.5 for Latin, Italian and English.
entries.limits: Wrong-language arm is one language (German for Latin), not a graded mismatch. Calibrated only for concatenative homophonic ciphers; null insertion and transposition untested. Preprint.
entries.ideas_for_us: Adopt the real-minus-surrogate differential: run every attack also on a ciphertext drawn from an order-k generator fitted to the same corpus, and report the gap. Their numbers give one external data point for a far-mismatch cell (Latin text, German model) to check against our boundary.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Should change the plan modestly: add a fitted-surrogate null (order-k generator matched to each real corpus) next to PC3's shuffled negative, and report recovery as real-minus-surrogate. Their wrong-language result (0-23.4% recovery) is consistent with a low plateau under mismatch.

entries.title: Can Statistics Tell Whether an Undeciphered Text Is Language? Calibrated Tests on the Voynich Manuscript
entries.question: Give both explanations the same effort, then judge them on text neither has seen.
entries.tried: They wrote the two main accounts of the Voynich manuscript, meaningless copying and an enciphered language, as programs that fill the manuscript's pages and lines word by word.
entries.method_data: Every program drew new words from the same word models and got the same search budget, and every cipher had a copying scribe so that local repetition favoured neither side. They fitted the programs to one set of statistics and judged them on 15 held-out statistics that no program was fitted to. They built a language signal that needs no decipherment: whether word pairs that share a line recur together in lines elsewhere in the book, calibrated on 28 texts in 16 languages and on ciphers of those texts with known miscopying. They ran solvers only after checking that each solver could read controls enciphered the way it assumes, and they planted hidden messages to measure what a search could still miss.
entries.key_results: The Timm and Schinner copying program misses none of the 15 held-out statistics by more than five standard deviations, while one-key word and Naibbe ciphers miss one by more than a hundred (section 4.3, p. 10). The statistic that separates them is the glyph-pair difference between Currier A and B pages: 0.093 bits in the manuscript, against 0.003 to 0.005 predicted by one-key ciphers (section 4.3, p. 10). Ciphers with two keys, or that encode only word classes, fit as well as copying; no program passes the joint check over all 37 statistics (section 4.3, pp. 10-12). The word-pair replication of 28 natural texts lies between 0.139 and 0.411; the manuscript reaches 0.071 in one transliteration and 0.053 in the other (section 5.1, p. 16). Word and syllable codes keep 52 to 84 percent of their plaintext's word-pair replication at the fitted miscopying rate and 11 to 23 percent at 60 percent miscopying (section 5.1, p. 17). Four published measures of language, including the conditional entropy of Rao et al. 2009 and Sproat's repetition share, cannot separate copying programs from language texts, because copying also makes text regular (sections 1 and 5.4, Table 6). One cipher stays open, a two-key nomenclator whose scribe miscopies more than half the words, and only for Arabic and Hebrew (sections 9 and 10). The authors say the word-pair test suits long texts with word breaks and gives the short, undivided Indus inscriptions little to count (section 9, 'Other undeciphered texts', p. 35).
entries.limits: The core rule, equal search effort for each account and judgement on statistics left out of the fit, is sound and transfers to any undeciphered corpus. Every negative result is backed by controls that the same test reads, which is what turns a failed decipherment into evidence. The copying programs were built from close study of the manuscript, so they bring knowledge the ciphers lack, as the authors admit (Limitations). Results hold only for the ciphers, languages and solvers tried; the solvers use bigram models and cannot read some controls, such as Hebrew. No code or data link is given in the paper, so the programs cannot be rerun as they stand.
entries.ideas_for_us: The equal-effort, held-out rule is now our standard for any reopened “language or code” test. Use a site-to-site divergence as a held-out statistic, the Indus analogue of the Currier A/B glyph difference: fit an emblem-slot generator, a copying generator and a word-sign language generator to Mohenjo-daro texts with equal budget, then score each on the sign-pair divergence between Mohenjo-daro and Harappa. (In the Voynich case this single held-out statistic separated one-key ciphers from copying by over a hundred standard deviations; a fixed-lexicon model and a drifting copy model make different predictions about between-site divergence.) Adapt the word-pair replication signal to whole texts: for non-adjacent sign pairs, compute their excess co-occurrence within texts against a shuffle that keeps first and last signs fixed, in two halves (alternating objects or two cities), and correlate the halves after removing near-copies. Run a planted-language power check first. (Language keeps recurring pairs across the corpus while copying makes only local pairs; the authors warn that short texts may give too little to count, so the power check decides whether it is worth running.)

entries.title: On automatic decipherment of lost ancient scripts relying on combinatorial optimisation and coupled simulated annealing
entries.question: Can a combinatorial optimiser with coupled simulated annealing beat neural decipherment at cognate matching on lost-script benchmarks, including new Cypriot, Phoenician and Luvian sets?
entries.tried: Encode the sign mapping as k-permutations (null, one-to-many and many-to-one allowed) and search it with coupled simulated annealing against an edit-distance cognate objective.
entries.method_data: Benchmarks: Ugaritic/Old Hebrew (2,214 cognate pairs; noisy version with unpaired words), Linear B/Mycenaean Greek (919 pairs) and a names-only variant, plus three new sets: Cypriot Syllabary/Arcadocypriot Greek (693 pairs, from Hintze 1993), Phoenician/Ugaritic, Luvian/Hittite (same script, different language). 16 parallel annealers; four runs per cell. Code: github.com/ftamburin/CSA_OptMatcher.
entries.key_results: Cognate accuracy (mean of four runs): Ugaritic/Hebrew noiseless 95.5, noisy 74.7; Phoenician/Ugaritic 80.5; Linear B/Greek 89.4, names-only 83.4; Cypriot/Arcadocypriot 86.3; Luvian/Hittite 47.5. A rerun of NeuroCipher with unrealistic information removed gives 90.4, 87.6, 71.2, 75.8, 67.9, 75.9 and 18.2 on the same sets. The author could not reproduce NeuroCipher's published figures.
entries.limits: Cognate identification only; no sign-value accuracy for its own system. No unrelated-language or graded-mismatch test. Partial known sign values are motivated but no experiment uses them. Needs segmented word lists.
entries.ideas_for_us: Use the released CS/AG and LB/MG cognate lists for stage-5 retrodiction as a second, lexicon-level check next to our running-text attack. The Luvian/Hittite cell (different language, same script) is a ready far-mismatch data point. Their k-permutation encoding is a way to allow many-to-one sign values in the logo-syllabic arm.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Does not change the core plan, but stage 5 should cite and reuse its Cypriot-Greek (693 pairs) and Linear B benchmarks, and note that its cognate accuracy drops to 47.5 when the known language is a different (if related) language.

entries.title: Decipherment as Regression: Solving Historical Substitution Ciphers by Learning Symbol Recurrence Relations
entries.question: Can a model trained on recurrence patterns decipher historical ciphers, even in another language?
entries.tried: Learn symbol recurrence relations, apply zero-shot, then add a few manual corrections.
entries.method_data: English-trained and 13-language models; the Latin Borg cipher.
entries.key_results: Applied zero-shot to the Latin Borg cipher, the English-trained model gives 45.14% symbol error. Three manual interventions bring it to 3.89%. A multilingual model gets 4.10% against 5.47% for an earlier system.
entries.limits: One alphabetic cipher; anecdotal, no dose-response.
entries.ideas_for_us: A striking single anchor point (3 fixes) to place on our anchor exchange-rate curve.

entries.title: Semantic scope of Indus inscriptions comprising taxation, trade and craft licensing, commodity control and access control
entries.question: What did the inscriptions do in Indus administration?
entries.tried: Inscriptions are licences and commodity-control marks, not personal names or toponyms.
entries.method_data: Archaeological contexts of seals near workshops and weights; Lothal sealings.
entries.key_results: Seals cluster near lapidary, metal and shell workshops and near weights; e.g. the Chanhu-daro bead factory room 215 held 14 weights, scale pans and seal C-22. Lothal sealing texts recur on Lothal seals (L-208/L-6, L-210/L-37).
entries.limits: Partial read. Interpretive; no nulls.
entries.ideas_for_us: Test fish-sign enrichment at lapidary sites against a site-size null (survey idea 4).

entries.title: The Decipherment of Linear Elamite Writing
entries.authors: Desset, Tabibzadeh, Kervran, Basello and Marchesi
entries.question: The most recent ancient script to be read, and a model of what the Indus script is missing.
entries.tried: Desset and colleagues gathered the 40 Linear Elamite texts known in 2021 (Table 1) and a glyph list, recording which texts each glyph occurs in (section 2.1, Fig. 3).
entries.method_data: They chose 9 cuneiform inscriptions of the same rulers and the same object types, mostly inscribed silver and copper beakers, as the known side (Table 2, section 2.2). They did not have true bilinguals: the Puzur-Sušinak cuneiform and Linear Elamite texts share names and titles but never translate each other (section 2.3). Starting from older correct readings and from expected names (Insušinak, Puzur-Sušinak, then the rulers Šilhaha, Eparti and the god Napireša on the Kam-Firuz beakers), they read the signs in 13 steps, each step adding names, titles and set phrases that recur in Elamite royal inscriptions in cuneiform (section 2.3, Fig. 5). They then described the system: an alpha-syllabary of vowels, consonants and CV signs, with homophones, defective spellings and a dividing sign (section 3).
entries.key_results: Through the 13 steps they read 72 signs with 73 values, which cover 96.3% of the 1,890 sign occurrences; 70 occurrences (about 3.7%) of 4 rare signs and 33 hapax signs remain unread (section 2.3, p. 32). The grid works with 77 values: 5 vowels, 12 consonants and 60 CV syllables (section 5, p. 52); no logograms or determinatives have been detected (section 2.3, note 27). They estimate the sign inventory at 80 to 110, slightly high because of unidentified graphic variants (section 3, before 3.2). They find 15 apparently homophonic pairs and one triplet; 3 pairs are probably graphic variants and 3 are true homophones (section 3.3). The key Kam-Firuz beakers were hypothesised to carry the names Šilhaha, Eparti and Napireša because of their supposed historical background, since none of them bears both scripts (section 2.3, p. 32). Two of the 40 texts are Gulf-type round stamp seals: V, a steatite seal of 3 signs (Ligabue collection), and G′, a gold round stamp seal of 6 signs (Table 1, group 7). They propose that Proto-Elamite and Linear Elamite are two stages of one 'Proto-Iranian' writing, and note that the Indus script is probably mixed phonographic and logographic given its number of signs (section 5).
entries.limits: The method is the classic one: proper names and standard royal phrases on dated, same-type objects give many sign values that check each other across texts. The anchors were partly assumed: the names on the Kam-Firuz beakers were expected from the objects' supposed origin, and most of these beakers come from a private collection rather than regular excavations (Table 1). The corpus is tiny, 40 texts and 1,890 sign occurrences, which the authors say is why a complete decipherment cannot yet be claimed. The approach needed a known language (Elamite) with long cuneiform texts of the same rulers; the Indus case has neither. Later critiques were not read here, so how far specialists accept the values is not assessed in this summary.
entries.ideas_for_us: This is why we search for names of people from the Indus region in cuneiform records, and asked museums for seal impressions on tablets that name them. Use Linear Elamite as a known-answer bench for the project's structural tools: from sign sequences alone, can they recover an alpha-syllabary with about 80-110 signs, few logograms, a divider and homophone pairs, at a corpus of 1,890 tokens? (It is the only recently read script at Indus scale; if the tools cannot recover its type, their Indus verdicts on script type carry little weight.) Copy their duplicate-alignment step: align Indus texts that recur on several independent objects (not moulded copies) and differ in one slot, and test whether the differing signs are closer in shape than random sign pairs of matched frequency. (In Linear Elamite the composite text F//G//H and other duplicates exposed graphic variants and homophones; this is a language-free way to find allographs that is different from the perplexity test in atlas 7.7.)

entries.title: Deciphering Undersegmented Ancient Scripts Using Phonetic Prior
entries.authors: Luo, Hartmann, Santus, Barzilay and Cao
entries.question: Can scripts without word boundaries be deciphered, and how much does the closeness of the known language matter?
entries.tried: Match spans of the lost text to a known lexicon with an IPA prior, against known languages of decreasing closeness, with and without a few known character values.
entries.method_data: Gothic against Proto-Germanic, Old Norse and Old English; Ugaritic; Iberian personal names. A 'partial' model knows 7 character values.
entries.key_results: Gothic A@10 at 0% whitespace: Proto-Germanic 0.820, Old Norse 0.213, Old English 0.046. Seven known characters lift Old Norse from 0.213 to 0.397 and Old English from 0.046 to 0.204. A closeness measure ranks the right family for Gothic and Ugaritic; for Iberian no language stands out.
entries.limits: One anchor set of 7, so no dose-response. No corpus-size sweep. Cognate span matching, not full sign-value recovery.
entries.ideas_for_us: This is the closest prior work to the mismatch study. Reproduce its Gothic closeness gradient on our pipeline as an alphabetic control, and extend its one anchor point to a dose-response (0, 5, 10, 20, 40).

entries.title: Neural Decipherment via Minimum-Cost Flow: from Ugaritic to Linear B
entries.question: Can a neural model match cognates between a lost and a known language, including Linear B and Greek?
entries.tried: Character-level sequence-to-sequence model trained by casting word matching as minimum-cost flow, with monotonic and residual priors.
entries.method_data: Ugaritic/Hebrew and Linear B/Greek cognate lists (Linear B 919 tokens), including a names-only Linear B set.
entries.key_results: Cognate identification: Ugaritic 93.5 (noiseless) and 65.9 (noisy); Linear B 84.7 and 67.3 on Linear B/names. Removing the monotonic or residual part gives 0.0; removing flow gives 8.6.
entries.limits: Cognate matching over lexicons that largely contain the answers, not sign-value recovery from running text. Known-language proximity is not varied.
entries.ideas_for_us: Its Linear B/names subset is a model for a names-only anchor test, which is the only anchor the Indus script could plausibly get.

entries.title: Interrogating Indus inscriptions to unravel their mechanisms of meaning conveyance (with 2021 and 2023 papers)
entries.question: Stroke signs as units of measure, crop signs as goods, and no personal names.
entries.tried: In 2019 Mukhopadhyay analysed sign combinations by hand in the Mahadevan corpus as enhanced in 1980 (IDF-80), counting distinct inscription-lines rather than objects.
entries.method_data: She sorted signs into functional classes, such as lexemes, phrase-final signs, connectives, numerals, crop signs and metrological signs, using where signs stand alone, where they end lines and which signs never occur together. In 2021 she argued from words outside the script: Akkadian, Hurrian and Old Persian words for elephant and ivory were borrowed from an Indus word pīlu, which she derives from a Proto-Dravidian word for tooth. In 2023 she combined script-internal patterns with find contexts (city gates, craft areas, weights, warehouse sealings, the Kanmer pendants) to argue that seals and tablets served taxation, licensing, trade control and access control. The 2025 SSRN paper proposing fish = maṇi 'gem' could not be opened, so it is not summarised here.
entries.key_results: 2019: 79% of the 2,906 inscribed objects in IDF-80 carry a single line of text, and about 70% of distinct lines have 1-5 signs (Methods and structural analysis sections). 2019: of 1,998 usable distinct lines, 1,293 (65%) end in one of 12 phrase-final signs; she lists 22 numeral signs and 49 signs that stand alone as lexemes by four isolation criteria (28, 16, 9 and 2 signs). 2019: co-occurrence restrictions point to logograms; two crop signs occur in 162 and 137 lines but never together, no line has two of the PPF signs (309 lines), and PF1 occurs in 1,338 lines with only 41 having two copies (section on logographic nature). 2019: 254 signs were classified as lexemes or function signs and 163 left unclassified, of which 133 (81%) occur in 1-5 lines (classification section). 2021: she argues the loanword chain pīlu > Akkadian pīru/pīri and Old Persian pîruš shows that many Indus people used a Proto-Dravidian tooth-word, so a significant part of the population spoke ancestral Dravidian languages (Abstract; Conclusion). 2023: she argues the inscriptions encoded no personal names or place names, pointing to stroke + sign sequences that recur with many different stroke counts and to texts with several fish signs side by side (section 'Indus-inscriptions did not encode names of individual seal-owners'). 2023: ICIT holds around 600 tablets with one inscribed face and more than 800 with two to four faces; she reads the numerical and metrological expressions found almost only on reverse faces as fixed license fees or slabs, and the obverse as the licensed activity (section on reverse-side numerical expressions). 2023: ICIT records around 210 inscribed sealings, and she cites Kharakwal et al. 2012 (p. 832) for the Kanmer clay pendants as possible identity cards or passes (sealings and Kanmer sections).
entries.limits: The 2019 class analysis is careful and gives counts that can be checked directly against the same corpus. None of the co-occurrence claims is tested against a null; 'never together' for two signs of 162 and 137 lines may or may not be surprising, given that most lines are short. The 2023 functional reading rests on qualitative find-context arguments; the project's own administrative and toponym tests (atlas 5.1, 5.4) found no positive structure, which fits her 'no toponyms' point but not any specific office structure. The 2021 argument is about language, not the script, and depends on etymologies that specialists may contest; it gives no sign values. The fish = gem claim (2025) could not be checked here because SSRN blocked the request.
entries.ideas_for_us: A first test found no sign tied to a craft at two sites, but it had too little data to tell. The fish = gem prediction needs find spots from bead workshops, which we have asked excavators for. Put her class-exclusivity claims under a null: for each pair she reports as never co-occurring (the two crop signs, the PPF signs, repeated PF1), compute how often two signs of those frequencies would share a line by chance under a length- and position-preserving shuffle, on dev then held-out families. (Mutually exclusive slot fillers are a cheap, language-free signature of a paradigm or logogram class; her counts were never tested, and atlas 7.4 tested graphic modifiers, not these classes.) Test her license-slab reading of two-sided tablets: if the reverse expression is a fee tied to the licensed activity, tablets with the same obverse text should carry the same reverse expression more often than shuffled pairs, across sites and phases. (It is a direct prediction of the 2023 paper; atlas 5.1 P11 and 6.5 looked at whether reverse values are fixed, but not at obverse-reverse pairing consistency.)
entries.read_note: partial (full text of the 2019 Palgrave Communications article, the 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Communications article and the 2023 Humanities and Social Sciences Communications article, read from the open HTML pages; the 2023 article was read by section, with Abstract, the names, numerals, reverse-side tablets, craft-area, Kanmer and Conclusions sections read closely; the 2025 SSRN paper (5079207) returned 403 and was not read, not even its abstract)

entries.title: An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers (with Narasimhan et al. 2019)
entries.authors: Shinde et al.; Narasimhan et al.
entries.question: One ancient genome: no steppe ancestry, and close links to later South Indian populations.
entries.tried: Shinde and colleagues sampled 61 skeletons from the Rakhigarhi cemetery, about 1 km west of the town, and obtained usable genome-wide data from one individual, I6113 (Shinde et al., Results).
entries.method_data: Because the data showed signs of contamination, they kept only reads with ancient-DNA damage, leaving 31,760 SNPs, and compared I6113 with ancient and modern genomes using PCA, ADMIXTURE, qpAdm and qpGraph (Shinde et al., Results). Narasimhan and colleagues reported genome-wide data from 523 ancient individuals, mostly from Central Asia, Iran and northernmost South Asia, spanning the last 8,000 years (Narasimhan et al., summary and introduction). In that larger study they found 11 outliers at Gonur and Shahr-i-Sokhta whose ancestry differs from their neighbours, and called them the Indus Periphery Cline (Narasimhan et al., section on an ancestry profile widespread during the IVC). Neither paper studies the script; both discuss language only by linking ancestry to the later spread of language families.
entries.key_results: I6113 was a female with mitochondrial haplogroup U2b2, which today is nearly exclusive to South Asia (Shinde et al., Results). I6113 fits as a mixture of Iranian-related ancestry and ancestry related to Andamanese hunter-gatherers (73% ± 6% Iranian-related, p = 0.103), and forms a clade with the 11 periphery outliers (p = 0.42); together they are renamed the IVC Cline (Shinde et al., Results). The 11 outliers make up 25% of the 44 good-quality individuals from Gonur and Shahr-i-Sokhta, and none had detectable Anatolian farmer-related ancestry (Shinde et al., Results; Narasimhan et al., IVC section). The Iranian-related part of the IVC Cline split from the lineages of ancient Iranian hunter-gatherers, herders and farmers before they separated, before about 10,000 BCE if the Belt Cave individual is used; 94% of symmetry-test trees supported this (Shinde et al., Results, Fig. 3). Steppe ancestry reached BMAC sites by 2100 BCE and South Asia in the first half of the second millennium BCE, contributing up to 30% of the ancestry of modern South Asian groups (Narasimhan et al., summary and BMAC section). Narasimhan et al. suggest the Ancestral South Indians most likely spoke an early Dravidian language, and give two scenarios: proto-Dravidian spread by IVC people, or by the half of ASI ancestry from peninsular South Asia (Narasimhan et al., Discussion). Shinde et al. argue the results count against a spread of Indo-European languages into South Asia with farmers from Anatolia or the Iranian plateau (Shinde et al., Discussion).
entries.limits: The ancestry results are careful and replicated across several methods, and the one Rakhigarhi genome agrees with 11 independent periphery individuals. The Rakhigarhi result rests on one contaminated-then-filtered sample with 31,760 SNPs; the authors say one sample, or even 12, cannot fully characterise a cosmopolitan civilisation (Shinde et al., Discussion). The link from ancestry to language is an inference, and Narasimhan et al. leave open which of two populations carried proto-Dravidian. For the script, these papers narrow the plausible language families but give no sign values, no word list and no anchor text.
entries.ideas_for_us: Background only. It narrows the likely language families but gives no sign values. Treat the genetics as a prior, not evidence: write down, before any language test, how much the project's posterior on Dravidian versus other families may move from these papers, and check that no test result is reported as confirming a family when the test itself is at chance. (Atlas 1.9 and section 3 show the script cannot yet decide the family; the genetics can easily leak in as if it were a script result.) When the Rakhigarhi excavation's inscribed seals are published with context, add them and test whether an eastern city follows the same sign order and slot use as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, with power computed first. (The genome shows Rakhigarhi people shared ancestry with the periphery cline; the script question is whether the same writing grammar ran to the eastern edge, which site_signal (atlas 10b.5) tested only for Mohenjo-daro versus Harappa.)
entries.read_note: full text of both main articles (Shinde et al. 2019 Cell, from the open copy on the Reich lab site; Narasimhan et al. 2019 Science, from the open copy of the published version on the Reich lab site); the STAR Methods of Shinde et al. and the supplements of both were not read; cell.com itself returned 403 earlier and was not retried

entries.title: A Bayesian phylogenetic study of the Dravidian language family
entries.authors: Kolipakam V, Jordan FM, Dunn M, Greenhill SJ, Bouckaert R, Gray RD, Verkerk A
entries.question: How old is the Dravidian family and how did it split?
entries.tried: Bayesian phylogenetics of cognate-coded basic vocabulary elicited from native speakers.
entries.method_data: Lexical data from Dravidian languages; Bayesian dating of the tree.
entries.key_results: The family is about 4,500 years old. North, Central, South I and South II branches recovered; relationships among main branches uncertain.
entries.limits: Basic-vocabulary dating has wide error; a 4,500-year root is close to the Mature Harappan but does not place speakers in the Indus.
entries.ideas_for_us: The age suggests the Indus-period language, if Dravidian, would be pre-Proto-Dravidian, not Old Tamil. For the mismatch study, compare the script against reconstructed Proto-Dravidian rather than modern Tamil.

entries.title: Decipherment with a Million Random Restarts
entries.question: Is decipherment failure caused by search or by the model?
entries.tried: Run up to a million EM restarts and compare the best score with the gold key's score.
entries.method_data: Zodiac 408 cipher; synthetic ciphers.
entries.key_results: Zodiac: 1 restart gives 18%, 100 give 90%, gains saturate near 100. The gold-initialised key scores -1467.4 but the best of 1M restarts scores -1466.5, and accuracy falls from 92% to 89%. Across 100 synthetic ciphers with 10K restarts, mean accuracy is 75%.
entries.limits: Matched model only; no size sweep.
entries.ideas_for_us: The study's statistical-versus-computational split is their diagnosis scaled up by mismatch. Report the gold-vs-best score gap per cell exactly as they did.

entries.title: Dependency-Based Decipherment for Resource-Limited Machine Translation
entries.question: Can richer structure raise the ceiling of cross-language word decipherment?
entries.tried: Replace adjacent bigrams with dependency bigrams.
entries.method_data: Spanish deciphered into English at 10M and 100M tokens.
entries.key_results: The adjacent-bigram system plateaus quickly at 4.2% at 10M tokens. Dependency bigrams reach 24.6% at 10M and 27.0% at 100M, and 41% on the top 5k types.
entries.limits: Word-to-word translation with no true 1:1 key; no anchors.
entries.ideas_for_us: This is the prior result a reviewer will cite against 'flat with size'. The study must separate its sign-value plateau from this word-level one, and test whether a richer model (trigram, A1) raises the ceiling the way dependencies did.

entries.title: The westward transmission of Indus Valley sealing technology
entries.question: Round seals from the Gulf use Indus signs in combinations rarely seen at home.
entries.tried: Laursen examined the 'Gulf Type' round stamp seals of the end of the third millennium BC as a whole group (abstract).
entries.method_data: He used principal component analysis of seal shape to compare Gulf Type seals with Indus inscriptions against those without (abstract). He grouped Gulf Type seals found in the Indus Valley, Iran, Mesopotamia and Bahrain into morphological groups that seem to match different areas of production (abstract). He studied the Indus inscriptions on these seals, focusing on the unusual frequency of a prefixed 'twins' sign in the western inscriptions (abstract). He used a newly found seal with a pseudo-inscription to test the idea that the Gulf seals record a language other than the Harappans' (abstract).
entries.key_results: The shape of Gulf Type seals with Indus inscriptions is distinct from that of seals without inscriptions (abstract). Gulf Type seals from different regions fall into fairly discrete morphological groups, apparently from different production areas (abstract). The western inscriptions show an abnormal number of prefixed 'twins' signs (abstract; the counts are in the full paper, not read). The hypothesis that a language different from the Harappans' was written on these seals is reconfirmed by the pseudo-inscription seal (abstract). He concludes that breakaway Harappans working in the west invented the Gulf Type seal, and that from about 2050 BC the type became practically synonymous with Dilmun's merchant communities (abstract). No numbers can be reported here, because only the abstract was read.
entries.limits: Combining seal shape, find region and inscription is a strong design, because it ties text features to production groups rather than treating all foreign seals as one set. The 'different language' conclusion rests partly on one pseudo-inscription seal; a pseudo-inscription can also mean that some makers imitated signs without writing any language. The project's own red team confirmed the order-breaking on foreign texts (9 of 39 flagged, binomial p = 1.1e-4), and the project's context notes (experiments/context/RESULTS.md) say pseudo-script fits as well as a second language. The detailed counts, the group assignments and the PCA loadings could not be checked here.
entries.ideas_for_us: Our round-seal finding builds on this, and adds that round seals found in Indus cities break the order too. Separate 'another language' from 'pseudo-script': test whether the flagged Gulf texts share Gulf-only sign pairs with each other more often than texts generated by an imitator who draws Indus signs by frequency with no grammar. (A second language written with borrowed signs should create its own repeated pairs across seals; pure imitation should not. The project's context notes say both explanations currently fit equally well.) Test whether the order-breaking texts sit in particular production groups: if Laursen's 'breakaway Harappan' early seals follow home order and the later Dilmun seals do not, order-breaking should track his morphological groups and date. (It turns his chronology into a falsifiable prediction about the project's 9 flagged texts, and would show whether the break came with the move to Dilmun workshops.)
entries.read_note: abstract only (the PDF on harappa.com, the harappa.com content page and the Wiley page all returned 403, and were not retried by other means; Semantic Scholar has the abstract withheld by the publisher; the abstract was read from the OpenAlex record; the paper is not open access per OpenAlex)

entries.title: A Statistical Model for Lost Language Decipherment
entries.question: Can a lost language be deciphered from a non-parallel corpus of a related known language?
entries.tried: Learn the letter mapping and the cognate pairs together, using morphology and sparsity priors from Hebrew.
entries.method_data: Bayesian model; Ugaritic texts against a Hebrew lexicon with morphology; an HMM substitution baseline with a Hebrew character-trigram model.
entries.key_results: The HMM baseline with a related-language model recovers 22 of 30 Ugaritic letters (73.3%). The full model reaches 96.67%. Cognate translation reaches 60.42% of types against 28.82% for the baseline.
entries.limits: Alphabetic script of about 30 letters. No corpus-size sweep and no graded relatedness. Many words have Hebrew cognates.
entries.ideas_for_us: Use the 73% related-model alphabet result as a calibration point for the alphabet arm of the mismatch study: our pipeline should land near it for Ugaritic with Hebrew.

entries.title: Lost Language Decipherment (thesis chapter)
entries.question: How much do cognates, morphology and the choice of known language matter for deciphering Ugaritic?
entries.tried: Ablate the model's parts and swap Hebrew for an unrelated language (English).
entries.method_data: Ablations of the 2010 model; candidate-mapping coverage and cross-character entropy for Hebrew vs English.
entries.key_results: Knowing the cognate set raises word-type accuracy to 71% against 63% for the full model; without morphology it scores 21%. Hebrew gives candidate mappings for 67% of Ugaritic words (4,797 / 7,386), English for 7% (551 / 7,386). Cross-character entropy is 0.48 for Hebrew and 1.58 for English.
entries.limits: Two languages only, not a graded scale. No size curve and no anchors.
entries.ideas_for_us: Cross-character entropy (0.48 vs 1.58) is a ready-made mismatch scalar; check whether it orders our language pairs the same way as excess cross-entropy.

entries.title: Entropic evidence for linguistic structure in the Indus script (with Sproat 2010 reply)
entries.authors: Rao, Yadav, Vahia, Joglekar, Adhikari and Mahadevan; Sproat
entries.question: A measure of how predictable the next sign is put Indus near languages. Critics showed non-writing scores there too.
entries.tried: Rao and colleagues computed the conditional entropy of the next sign given the previous one, with Kneser-Ney smoothing, for the Indus texts and for several languages, DNA, protein, Fortran and two artificial 'non-linguistic' systems.
entries.method_data: Their two non-linguistic controls were generated by the authors: one with every sign equally likely to follow any other, one with each sign having a single fixed successor. Sproat (2010) replied that those two controls describe no real symbol system, and showed that a random corpus with Zipf-like sign frequencies and no sequential structure reproduces the Indus curve. Sproat also tested the Pictish entropy classifier of Lee, Jonathan and Ziman on Mesopotamian kudurru deity symbols and on dice rolls. Rao et al. (2010) answered that they never claimed entropy alone proves language, extended the analysis to block entropies up to six signs, and framed the question as a Bayesian weight of evidence. Sproat (2014) built corpora of seven non-linguistic and fourteen linguistic systems and tested all proposed measures on them.
entries.key_results: Rao et al. used 1,548 lines and 7,000 sign occurrences from Mahadevan 1977, dropping texts with doubtful signs, multi-line texts and duplicates (Supplement, Datasets). Indus conditional entropy sat in the band of the language corpora, closest to Sumerian and Old Tamil, and far from the two artificial controls (Fig. 1). Indus perplexity drops from 68.82 for single signs to 26.69 for bigrams and only to 25.26 by n = 4-5, so most predictable structure is captured by sign pairs (Supplement, Table S1). Sproat reports that a 400-element Zipf distribution with alpha = 1.5 and independent bigrams fits the Indus result well (Sproat 2010, section 2, p. 589). On the Lee et al. measures, a kudurru corpus of 545 tokens and 59 types scores Cr = 8.0 and Ur = 1.55, and 75 dice-roll 'texts' of 638 symbols score Cr = 12.64 and Ur = 1.18, so both are classed as writing (pp. 591-592). Sproat 2014 abstract: none of the previously published methods is useful as published; one Lee et al. measure with a different cut-off and a new repetition-based measure do separate the two classes, and both put Indus and Pictish on the non-linguistic side (abstract only).
entries.limits: Sproat's core criticism holds: Rao's non-linguistic controls were synthetic extremes, and a frequency-matched random baseline lands in the language band. Rao's narrower point, that Indus sign order is far from random and far from rigid, is true but was already known. Sproat 2014's positive result rests on a small number of systems and on cut-offs fitted to them; with about 20 labelled systems a classifier can easily overfit, and the project's own calibration (language_vs_code) found no metric reliable at Indus size. Both sides treat the Indus corpus as one genre; mixing seals, tablets and pots may move any statistic.
entries.ideas_for_us: Treat entropy, Zipf and n-gram arguments as closed in both directions. Run the same entropy and repetition measures separately on Indus genres (square seals, bar seals, moulded tablets, incised tablets, pots), each against a genre-matched null. (The whole debate treats Indus as one corpus; if genres differ strongly, some apparent 'language-like' or 'code-like' signal is a mixture effect.) Add Sproat's released non-linguistic corpora (kudurrus, totem poles, barn stars and others) to the project's calibration set, if the files are still online and licensed for reuse. (The calibration set had only six codes; more real codes would make the posterior sharper or show it cannot move.)

entries.title: Attacking Decipherment Problems Optimally with Low-Order N-gram Models
entries.question: How does exact decipherment error fall with cipher length for different n-gram models?
entries.tried: Solve decipherment exactly with integer programming, removing search error.
entries.method_data: English substitution ciphers of 2-256 letters; 1-, 2- and 3-gram English models.
entries.key_results: With 3-grams, decipherment works well on ciphers of 64 letters or more. At 414 letters with a 2-gram model, EM gives 10% error and the exact method 0.5%. Shannon unicity is 173, 74 and 50 letters for the 1-, 2- and 3-gram models.
entries.limits: The plaintext model always matches the text. No mismatch.
entries.ideas_for_us: The template for 'recovery against size with search error removed'. Our matched-model control should reproduce its shape before any mismatch cell counts.

entries.title: Unsupervised Analysis for Decipherment Problems
entries.question: How do EM-based decipherment methods behave across tasks and source models?
entries.tried: Decipher a Spanish text against 80 different source-language models.
entries.method_data: Don Quixote ciphertext; phoneme and letter models for 80 languages; EM with restarts.
entries.key_results: Final edit distance: Spanish 434, Galician 741, Portuguese 1487, Kurdish 4041, English 4116. The correct language still wins on likelihood. The authors describe EM locking onto the right theory and then drifting as it fits the model's bigram frequencies.
entries.limits: No size sweep under mismatch, no true-key score test, no anchors. Alphabetic only.
entries.ideas_for_us: Reproduce the Spanish/Galician/Portuguese ladder as an alphabetic mismatch control on our pipeline.

entries.title: The Collapse of the Indus-Script Thesis: The Myth of a Literate Harappan Civilization
entries.question: Texts are very short, and many signs are rare: maybe these are symbols, not a script.
entries.tried: Farmer, Sproat and Witzel reviewed the whole case for the Indus signs being writing and argued it had never been tested, only assumed.
entries.method_data: They set the length of Indus inscriptions against what literate societies leave on durable objects such as pots, walls, stelae and tablets. They compared sign frequencies in the Mahadevan and Wells catalogues with Sumerian, Egyptian, Chinese and Scottish heraldry blazons. They counted how often a sign repeats inside a single inscription, using 67 Mohenjo-daro seals and 67 Harappa seals matched in length to 67 Egyptian royal cartouches. They counted rare and one-off signs and argued, from Near Eastern emblem systems such as kudurru deity symbols, that the signs worked as non-linguistic symbols. They closed with five explicit conditions under which they would accept that their model is wrong.
entries.key_results: The longest text on one surface has 17 signs, fewer than 1 in 100 texts reach 10 signs, and the mean over 2,905 objects in Mahadevan's concordance is 4.6 signs (p. 22). Four of Mahadevan's 417 signs make up 21% of 13,372 sign occurrences, eight make up 31%, and twenty make up over 50% (p. 26). The cumulative frequency curve of Indus signs nearly overlaps that of heraldic blazons and Egyptian hieroglyphs, so they say sign frequency cannot separate scripts from non-scripts (pp. 27-29, Fig. 2). In length-matched samples, 67 Egyptian cartouches (465 signs) have 48 repeated signs within an inscription, against 8 in 67 Mohenjo-daro seals (495 signs) and 7 in 67 Harappa seals (493 signs) (p. 33, Table 1). The 78 Harappa bar-seal inscriptions in CISI vols. I-II contain one case of sign repetition, and bar seals date late, so they argue the system was not drifting toward sound-writing after about 600 years (p. 33). 27% of Mahadevan's 417 signs occur once and 52% occur five times or fewer; in Wells 1999, 50% of over 600 signs occur once and 75% five times or fewer (p. 36). They claim, from unpublished CISI vol. 3 material, that the share of one-off signs rises as new texts are found, the reverse of what a closed script should show (pp. 36-37). Their falsifiers: a text with evidence of several hundred signs; a 50+ sign text with random-looking repeats; a bilingual with about 30+ Indus signs; a rule set others can apply; or a lexical sign list (p. 48).
entries.limits: The brevity facts and the low within-text repetition are real and reproducible on the concordance. The repetition comparison uses one Egyptian genre (cartouches) as the only writing control, so it cannot tell short name-writing in a logographic script from non-writing. The rising-singleton claim rests on unpublished data and on sign-list choices that the authors themselves say are easily shifted (p. 37, n. 23). The paper argues for non-writing by analogy and rhetoric as much as by test, and later work (SIGIL, the project's own language_vs_code) shows these statistics do not decide the question either way.
entries.ideas_for_us: We test whether the signs are language at all, instead of assuming it. Test the rising-singleton claim directly: compare the share of one-off signs in M77 texts against ICIT texts first published after 1977, with sampling-size matched rarefaction curves and Chao1 estimates of total inventory. (A closed script should show the singleton share fall as the corpus grows; an open emblem system should not. FSW made the claim on unpublished data and nobody has run it with a null.) Rerun the within-text repetition count with length-matched controls drawn from short logographic name corpora (Ur III seal legends, Linear B personal-name lines) instead of Egyptian cartouches only. (The Table 1 contrast may reflect genre (names written logographically repeat little) rather than writing versus non-writing; the project already holds Ur III and Linear B lines.)
entries.read_note: full text

entries.title: A Computational Approach to Deciphering Unknown Scripts
entries.question: How much text is needed to decipher a script phonetically, and does script type matter?
entries.tried: Learn sign-to-sound mappings with EM given a sound model of the true language.
entries.method_data: Spanish, Japanese kana and Chinese, each with its true language model.
entries.key_results: Spanish: 100 sentences give 97.5%, 20 give 82.2%, 5 give 48.5%. Kana: 200 sentences give 99%. Chinese (logographic): 22% syllable accuracy against a 3.2% baseline, even with the true model.
entries.limits: They raise robustness to language change but never test it.
entries.ideas_for_us: Their 22% on logographic Chinese with a matched model clashes with our 'about 2,500 tokens suffice'. The logo-syllabic arm must report inventory size and logogram share so the two results can be reconciled.

entries.title: Deciphering the Indus Script (and Parpola 2010, A Dravidian solution)
entries.question: Fish sign = mīn, a word that means both “fish” and “star” in Dravidian languages.
entries.tried: Parpola first argues for the language: he rules out Indo-Aryan, Burushaski, Tibeto-Burman and Austro-Asiatic on historical grounds and concludes the Harappans probably spoke Dravidian.
entries.method_data: He argues for the script type from sign count: about 400 signs fits logo-syllabic writing and is too many for a syllabary or alphabet. He sets a four-part test for reading any sign: the pictured object is recognisable, the sign is used as a rebus, the context shows the intended meaning, and a Proto-Dravidian homophone exists in more than one subgroup. He starts from the fish sign, assumes seal texts hold personal names with divine elements as in Mesopotamia, and reads fish as min, 'fish' and 'star'. He then cross-checks readings like a crossword: signs that combine with fish or with each other must give compounds attested in Old Tamil.
entries.key_results: His sign list has very nearly 400 graphemes, separated by shape similarity plus similar context (p. 8). Fish signs, plain and modified, are so common on seals that almost every tenth sign belongs to the group, yet fish never appears in Mesopotamian seal legends, so he argues the fish is a rebus (p. 16). 6 + fish reads aru-min, the Old Tamil name of the Pleiades; 7 + fish reads elu-min, Ursa Major, and is the whole text of the large seal H-9 (p. 18). Fig tree + fish reads vata-min, 'north star', via vatam 'banyan' and vata 'north' (pp. 19-21). Two intersecting circles read muruku, both 'bangle/ear-ring' and the god Murukan; he cites the sign's high frequency on the 40 or more inscribed stoneware bangles, some of which carry only this sign (pp. 23-24). Intersecting circles is followed three times by a squirrel sign, read pillai 'young', matching the attested Tamil name Muruka-ppillai (pp. 26-27). Two long vertical strokes, which both follows intersecting circles and precedes fish, is read vel/vel, giving Muruka-vel and ven-min 'Venus'; he also argues from M-172 versus H-6 that this sign and fish substitute for each other in the same context (pp. 27-29). He judges these interlocking readings to exclude chance and says a full decipherment is not possible with the present material (pp. 14, 29).
entries.limits: The method is explicit and the readings make concrete distributional claims (fixed numeral + fish pairs, sign co-occurrence, object-specific signs) that can be checked. The cross-checks are judged by the author, with no null model for how often an arbitrary rebus chain would find attested Tamil compounds by chance. Several key cases rest on two or three texts (the M-112/M-241 pair, three squirrel texts, the M-172/H-6 substitution). The project's own tests already weaken parts of it: 7 + fish is depleted rather than fixed, 3 + fish failed held-out, and fish signs do not behave like god names.
entries.ideas_for_us: We turned his readings into predictions and tested them. Six + fish holds as a fixed unit; “seven stars” is not supported; the fish signs group together but do not behave like god names. Test Parpola's substitution claim that the two-tall-strokes sign (M87) and the plain fish (M59) fill the same slot: measure context overlap of M87 and M59 against frequency-matched sign pairs, on dev then held-out families. (It is a sharp internal prediction of the vel reading that does not need any language; the substitution machinery already exists in experiments/substitution.) Score the intersecting-circles (M403) object prediction with a null: is it over-represented on bangles and amulets relative to seals, after removing copies, and does M403 + M87 behave as a fixed unit like 6 + fish? (Parpola ties M403 to bangles and to a deity name; the bangle_oval work found no independent bangle sample, but the fixed-unit and amulet parts have not been closed.)

entries.title: The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables
entries.question: 417 signs, numbered, and every text then known. The M-numbers on this site come from it.
entries.tried: Mahadevan compiled every Indus inscription known to him into one numbered corpus, with a sign list and a concordance of every place each sign occurs (Yadav et al. 2010, Materials and Methods).
entries.method_data: He gave each sign a serial number, which later statistical work kept, so 'M342' in this project is his sign 342 (Yadav et al. 2010, Materials and Methods). He marked lost, damaged or illegible passages with diagonal lines and doubtful readings with an asterisk, which later users relied on to filter the texts (Yadav et al. 2010, Materials and Methods). He included tables of sign frequency and position; Farmer, Sproat and Witzel cite 'Mahadevan 1977: Table 1, 717-23' for positional regularities (FSW 2004, p. 21).
entries.key_results: The concordance records 417 unique signs in 3,573 lines of 2,906 texts (Yadav et al. 2010, Materials and Methods). It holds 13,372 sign occurrences; just four of the 417 signs make up 21% of them, eight make up 31%, and twenty over 50% (FSW 2004, p. 26). The average inscription in the concordance is 4.6 signs long (FSW 2004, p. 22). In the filtered EBUDS subset of 1,548 texts, sign 342 alone accounts for 10% of occurrences and 69 signs for about 80%, which the authors say is consistent with Mahadevan's earlier analysis of the full corpus (Yadav et al. 2010, Empirical Analysis). Text endings are more fixed than beginnings: 23 signs cover about 80% of text-ender use against 82 signs for text beginners (Yadav et al. 2010, Empirical Analysis, Fig. 4). Removing damaged, doubtful, multi-line and duplicate texts drops 40 of the 417 signs; 33 of those occur only once in M77 (Yadav et al. 2010, Materials and Methods). FSW 2004 argue that Duhoux and Mahadevan applied Mackay's sign-count formula to all 13,372 symbols instead of small samples; used that way it 'predicts' 540 signs, while samples of the right size give well under half of 417 (FSW 2004, p. 28).
entries.limits: The concordance is the shared reference for almost all statistical work, so results from different groups can be compared sign by sign. It is a 1977 snapshot: later finds, especially from Harappa after 1986 and from Dholavira, are not in it. Its sign list lumps or splits forms differently from Wells and Fuls, so any sign-level result can depend on the list used. Only secondary descriptions were read here, so details of the book's own tables and conventions are not reported first-hand.
entries.ideas_for_us: The backbone of our main transcription. Audit M77's doubtful readings: for every asterisked or damaged sign in M77, compare with the ICIT reading of the same object, and test whether an n-gram model trained on other families predicts the ICIT reading better than the M77 one. (Yadav et al. report restoration accuracy of about 74% under cross-validation; a known-answer check against an independent transcription shows how far the main corpus's uncertain signs can be trusted.) Run a sign-list sensitivity check on the project's surviving positive results: redo each one after removing or merging every sign where M77 and Wells disagree on splitting, and report which results move. (Mahadevan's 417 signs and Wells's larger list split forms differently; a result that depends on that choice is about the sign list, not the script.)
entries.read_note: partial (the 1977 book itself was not opened: harappa.com returned 403, no publisher open copy exists, and the only full copy found online is an unlicensed personal upload on archive.org, which I did not open; I read in full Yadav, Joglekar, Rao, Vahia, Adhikari and Mahadevan 2010, an open-access paper co-authored by Mahadevan that describes and uses the concordance, and reused the figures about it in Farmer, Sproat and Witzel 2004, already read in full for fsw-2004)

entries.title: Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems
entries.question: How much ciphertext does an attacker need before the key is determined?
entries.tried: Define equivocation and the unicity distance from the key entropy and the redundancy of the language.
entries.method_data: Information theory.
entries.key_results: Unicity distance is about H(K)/D, about 30 letters for English simple substitution. For some 'languages' equivocation does not approach zero however much text is intercepted. The analysis assumes the attacker knows the message probabilities.
entries.limits: Assumes a correct message model, which is exactly what fails under mismatch.
entries.ideas_for_us: Frame the plateau as a unicity distance that never arrives when the attacker's model is wrong; state the condition formally as a cross-entropy gap.

entries.title: Stoicheia: Character-Level Masked Diffusion for Ancient Greek Textual Restoration, Parsing, and Metrical Scansion
entries.question: Does character-level masked-diffusion pretraining improve restoration of damaged Greek inscriptions and other tasks?
entries.tried: A 405M-parameter character-level masked-diffusion encoder with separately maskable planes (letters, boundaries, diacritics, capitals, punctuation); every experiment has a random-initialisation control.
entries.method_data: Open, revision-pinned corpus of 380M words; ten decontaminated folds so each passage is unseen by at least one released model; Ithaca test split.

entries.limits: Abstract only; known language with a huge corpus.
entries.ideas_for_us: Decontaminated rotated folds and matched random-init controls are good practice for our restoration benchmark.

entries.title: The Undeciphered Aegean Scripts (incl. ch. 7 'Syllabotactic Analysis' and ch. 11 on Cypro-Minoan)
entries.question: Can statistics on syllable combinations (syllabotactics) tell whether two undeciphered syllabic scripts write the same language, without reading them?
entries.tried: Syllabotactic comparison of Linear A, Cretan Hieroglyphic, Phaistos, Cypro-Minoan and Eteocypriot, with Cypriot Syllabic vs. Linear B as a known control.
entries.method_data: Book with all data included; chapter-level analyses (abstract only seen; no numbers in the abstract).
entries.key_results: Control: Cypriot Syllabic vs. Linear B gives an 'overwhelming probability' of the same language. Linear A does not encode Greek, nor does Eteocypriot. Cypro-Minoan and Linear A encode different languages; Cypro-Minoan and Eteocypriot encode the same language.
entries.limits: Only chapter abstracts read; method details and error rates unknown to us. Relies on shared sign values across scripts.
entries.ideas_for_us: A reading-free 'same language?' test is effectively a mismatch detector. Validate it on our known pairs: does its score track our excess cross-entropy? If so it could estimate mismatch for Linear A or Cypro-Minoan candidates.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Could supply an independent mismatch measure for real scripts in stage 5; worth a check on training pairs, not a plan change.

entries.title: Linear Elamite Texts from Susa (OrientLab SM 10)
entries.question: All the Susa texts of the script read in 2022, the most recent ancient script to be read.
entries.tried: Desset and colleagues proposed a phonetic reading of Linear Elamite, anchored on proper names shared with cuneiform Elamite texts (from the item summary; the paper itself was not read).
entries.method_data: The Hatamti database publishes each Linear Elamite document with a sign-by-sign transliteration and translation, citing the 2026 edition volume by Desset, Tabibzadeh, Basello and Marchesi. That volume, 'Linear Elamite Inscriptions and Related Cuneiform Texts, Vol. 1: Linear Elamite Texts from Susa', gives full editions of the Susa texts (Hatamti citation).
entries.key_results: Hatamti document 6 (Sb 155) has 50 signs and is read as naming Puzur-Sušinak, king of Awan, with the phrase 'Insušinak loves him'; its edition is in section 3.4.1, pp. 85-91 of the 2026 volume (Hatamti doc 6). Hatamti document 2 (Sb 6) has 33 signs and runs left to right; its edition is in section 3.3.1, pp. 71-79 (Hatamti doc 2). No figures from the ZA paper are reported here because it was not read.
entries.limits: Linear Elamite now has a public sign-by-sign corpus with readings, which makes it a rare known-answer test for statistical methods. The reading rests on a small corpus of a few dozen texts and on name anchors, and is not accepted by all specialists; this record cannot weigh that because the paper was not read. Our own crib test with Linear Elamite as a known answer was negative (experiments/crib_le_known_answer).
entries.ideas_for_us: We used Linear Elamite as a known-answer test for our own name-matching method. The method could not recover its values, so we stopped it rather than run it on Indus. Use the Hatamti Linear Elamite transliterations as a known-answer bench: run each of our structural methods (positional classes, sign clustering, restoration) blind on the Linear Elamite sign strings and score them against the published readings. (A method that cannot recover known syllable classes or word breaks in a small, deciphered corpus should not be trusted on Indus.) Measure how short Linear Elamite texts must be cut before the methods fail, by truncating texts to Indus lengths. (It gives a power curve for methods on texts of four to five signs.)

entries.title: Constructional Grammar and Semantic Constraints in the Indus Script
entries.question: A paper on sign grammar makes one sharp claim that can be checked in minutes.
entries.tried: The author collapsed a Wells-coded working corpus into 2,022 distinct sequence families with 9,302 sign occurrences, so repeated texts are not counted twice.
entries.method_data: He added nine fixed two-sign contexts to a bigram model and tested whether they improve prediction on held-out sites, leaving out test families seen in training. He screened for frames that hold in both Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, using one city to find them and the other to check them. He recounted specific contrasts, such as which signs follow W520 and W740, and the order of numerals and nouns by object type. He kept a ledger that assigns a functional role to each token and reports its coverage, while calling these roles interpretations, not translations.
entries.key_results: Adding the nine contexts lowers held-out negative log-likelihood from 4.33935 to 4.32551 over 6,778 predictions, a gain of 0.01384 nats with 95% interval 0.00979 to 0.01789 (abstract; section 4.1, p. 5). Three of five archived construction tasks survived correction, the strongest being W590 frame completion with a gain of 0.3056 over 199 events (Table 1, p. 5). Two new cross-city frames passed: W920-W060-W741 (Harappa 3/6, Mohenjo-daro 18/30) and W840-W032-W740 (6/6, 10/11) (section 4.1, p. 5). Excluding W033-led cases, W090 follows W520 in 0 of 136 cases and W740 in 69 of 994, two-sided Fisher p = 0.00017674; without W220 families it is 0/86 against 52/876, p = 0.01099 (section 4.2, Table 2, p. 6). Numerals precede nouns 277 times and follow them 59 times; postnominal order is 11.0% of seal pairs, 31.1% of tablet pairs and 64.3% of pottery pairs (section 4.3, p. 6). W590 before the W390 family goes on to W740 in 33 of 46 cases on square seals against 0 of 128 without W590 (Table 3, p. 7). The role ledger covers 7,846 of 9,302 tokens (84.347%) and fully assigns 1,004 of 2,022 families (section 4.6). Base sign forms are followed by a resolver in 74 of 692 cases against 0 of 50 for caged forms, but this weakens to nominal p = 0.0974 once terminal cases are dropped (section 5, p. 9).
entries.limits: The author is frank: he says the contexts were chosen during earlier work, so the held-out gain is not an independent test, and the p values are uncorrected. The overall gain over a bigram is tiny, and he notes it has not been compared with a tuned trigram or four-gram model. The corpus files are withheld, so nobody else can rerun the corpus-level numbers; only the code and aggregates are public. Many results are sharp zero cells such as 0/136; our own test found such zero cells common in Indus sign order (24 of 57 similar triples), so sharpness alone is weak evidence. Semantic labels such as FISH, TREE and POT rest on sign shape and are not tested against anything external.
entries.ideas_for_us: We tested it. The pattern shows in reading order on the main texts, but not on texts kept aside, and gaps this sharp are common: 24 of 57 similar sign pairs have one. So it is real but not special. Test the two cross-city frames (W920-W060-W741 and W840-W032-W740) and the W590-W390-W740 frame on our family-clean held-out M77 split and on ICIT sites outside Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, translated through the Wells-to-Mahadevan bridge. (These were found with a city-split procedure and are the author's most portable claims; we only tested the W090 contrast so far.) Replicate the numeral-noun order shift by object type (postnominal 11% on seals, 31% on tablets, 64% on pottery) on M77 held-out texts with a family-level permutation null. (If word order follows the object, that is a register effect worth separating from grammar, and it fits the project's finding that each object type has its own vocabulary.)

entries.title: Positional constraints, sequence uniqueness and stroke numerals in Indus seals of Mohenjo-daro
entries.question: They argued seal texts work like ID numbers. On 646 seals, the texts repeat more than chance, not less.
entries.tried: The author took 179 unicorn seals from Mohenjo-daro (M-1 to M-199) from a public GitHub transcription of the corpus.
entries.method_data: He measured how many sign sequences are unique and compared this with a permutation null. He measured sign entropy by position in five-sign texts and tested whether it differs between positions. He counted stroke signs by position, looked for near-identical pairs one sign apart, and counted prefix-sharing groups. He interprets the seals as a registration-code system rather than language.
entries.key_results: The corpus has 1,003 tokens and 182 sign types (section 3). Uniqueness is 98.3% (176 of 179) against a null of 91.2%, with interval 88.7 to 93.5 (section 5.1, p. 9). In 35 five-sign texts, entropy by position is 3.13, 4.44, 4.45, 3.77 and 3.98 bits; Friedman chi-squared 14.7, p = 0.005, Kendall W 0.105 (section 5.2). Stroke signs are 154 of 1,003 tokens (15.4%) and make up 45.7% of position 4 in five-sign texts, chi-squared 27.4 (section 5.4). The two-stroke sign is 103 of 154 stroke tokens (66.9%); the PDF gives chi-squared 198.3 while the abstract gives 225.3 (section 5.5 and abstract). Eight pairs differ by one sign, all at positions 2 or 3, p = 0.008 (section 5.6). There are 28 prefix-sharing groups, and the author claims a capacity of 1.35 million codes (section 5.7).
entries.limits: The paper states clear falsification tests, which makes its claims checkable. The sample is small (179 seals, 35 five-sign texts), from one site and one animal. The chi-squared value for the two-stroke sign differs between abstract and text. The uniqueness null depends on how texts are permuted; our own run on 646 seals found observed uniqueness below the null, reversing the sign of the result (experiments/bench2026).
entries.ideas_for_us: Nothing to borrow. Their best result was already known, and the rest fails. Test whether the sign vocabulary depends on the animal motif: compare sign distributions on bull, unicorn and other-motif seals with a family-level permutation null that keeps text length. (A registration code should be indifferent to the motif, while a title or office system would vary with it; the author lists this as a falsification test.) Compare the positional entropy profile of seals and tablets, by text length, with family dedup. (The author predicts divergence between seals and tablets; this is cheap and uses the whole corpus rather than 35 texts.)

entries.title: Regional bio-mobility of bovines during the Harappan period: Evidence from C-O-Sr isotopes of faunal bioapatite at Kanmer and Tigrana
entries.authors: Mahala MK, Laskar AH, Goyal P, Kharakwal JS, Parmar N, Rawat Y, Lamba A, Kanungo AK, et al.
entries.question: Did Harappan cattle and sheep/goat move between regions, and does that show trade?
