entries.title: How Non-Linguistic Is the Indus Sign System? A Synthetic-Baseline Scorecard
entries.question: Compared with made-up systems of known kinds, Indus falls between heraldry and administrative records.
entries.tried: The authors took the ICIT sign codes through the Yajnadevam digitization and removed exact duplicate texts.
entries.method_data: They built two synthetic non-linguistic baselines, a heraldic system and an administrative system, with generators tuned to Indus-like length and frequency. They scored Indus and both baselines on a five-measure scorecard: text length, repeated phrases, hapax rate, positional rigidity and related statistics. They ran sensitivity checks over generator settings, merged likely allographs, and compared Indus with real non-linguistic corpora such as heraldic blazons.
entries.key_results: The corpus has 2,511 texts, of which 595 (24%) are exact duplicates, leaving 1,916 texts with 11,110 tokens, 584 sign types and a mean length of 4.4 (section 3). Conditional entropy is 3.232 bits against a shuffle mean of 4.613, and the Zipf slope is -1.49 (section 5.2). On the scorecard, Indus, heraldic and administrative values are: length 4.42, 4.01 and 4.02; repeated 3+ sign phrases 565, 310 and 339; repeated 5+ sign phrases 43, 25.7 and 9.0 (Table 4, section 5.3). Hapax rate is 0.33, 0.10 and 0.44, and positional rigidity is 0.15, 0.08 and 0.23, so Indus lies between the two baselines only on these two measures (Table 4). Against the administrative baseline the result holds in 10 of 11 settings for hapax rate, 5 of 11 for rigidity and 8 of 11 for repetition (Table 5). Merging 200 likely allographs lowers the hapax rate from 33.2% to 21.1% (Table 6). Real heraldic blazons (SCA) match Indus rigidity at 0.149, but no real non-linguistic system matches all measures (Table 8, section 5.7). The heraldic generator misses its own Zipf target, giving -0.97 against -1.46 (Table 2).
entries.limits: Using two different non-linguistic baselines and real heraldic data is a fair design, and the sensitivity tables are reported. Indus is above both baselines on length and on repeated phrases, so the 'intermediate' reading holds only for two of five measures. Only exact duplicates were removed, so near-copy formulas still inflate the repetition counts. The hapax and rigidity results depend on sign segmentation, as the allograph merge shows, and artifact type was not conditioned on (section 7). The abstract says code and data are public, but the availability section says they will be released on request or upon acceptance.
entries.ideas_for_us: Agrees with our finding that each kind of object has its own vocabulary. Nothing new to run. Rerun the five-measure scorecard on M77 with near-copy families collapsed and separately for seals, tablets and pottery, adding SIGIL as a third baseline. (It shows whether the 'between heraldry and administration' pattern survives family dedup and object type, which the authors list as their main gap.) Compute the scorecard on ICIT and M77 side by side for the same objects to measure how much each number moves with the sign list alone. (Hapax rate fell from 33.2% to 21.1% after allograph merging, so sign-list choice may decide the verdict.)

entries.title: Reconstruction of Geometric and Structural Aspects of Undeciphered Messages by Information-theoretic Methods
entries.question: Which structural relations (layout, segmentation, reading direction) can be recovered from undeciphered records without any proposed reading?
entries.tried: Apply algorithmic-information and predictive-coding measures with held-out records and matched nulls to Phaistos, khipu, Rongorongo, Indus and Voynich, with Egyptian and Arecibo as controls.
entries.method_data: Indus: a derivative inscription CSV; 75 unique multiline sequences out of 5,679 records; Mohenjo-daro held out; 292 gaps in 47 inscriptions, 49 of them row breaks. Naive-Bayes break prediction; 999 null draws; object bootstrap.
entries.key_results: Indus row-break prediction reaches AUC 0.812 (interval 0.742-0.871) but a code gain of only 0.0092 bits per gap. Rongorongo gives AUC 0.51; Egyptian 0.95. Phaistos keeps 0.714 bits of excess adjacent-sign mutual information after positional controls. The authors warn that any search over languages, mappings and settings must sit inside the train/test separation.
entries.limits: Indus test is small (47 inscriptions) and uses slash delimiters from a derivative CSV, not measured coordinates. Says nothing about sign values.
entries.ideas_for_us: Report both ranking (accuracy) and calibrated probability (bits) for every attack, since they can disagree sharply. Their rule that language and model selection must be held out matches our sealed held-out families.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: No change. It supports keeping the language choice inside the held-out protocol and reporting score-based (bits) measures next to accuracy.

entries.title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
entries.question: Which statistical regularities of cuneiform belong to the shared script and which to each language (Akkadian, Sumerian, Elamite)?
entries.tried: Compare two dictionary-free segmenters (transitional probability vs. Morfessor) within and across languages, and combine Unicode and Latin-transliteration features for tagging.
entries.method_data: ORACC Akkadian, ETCSL Sumerian, Elamite (Elamite Dictionary plus Utunasu); six cross-language transfer pairs; learning curves; a Hittite stress test with foreign-script logograms.
entries.key_results: Both segmenters reach F1 above 0.97 within language, against 0.74 for the dictionary MaxMatch baseline. Transitional probability keeps F1 above 0.95 across all six language pairs, while Morfessor collapses to F1 0.27 when trained on the 13K-token Elamite source. On Hittite, with 34.7% foreign-script logograms, transitional probability drops 35 points and Morfessor 8. Concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks.
entries.limits: Segmentation and tagging, not decipherment. Training needs segmented text in a source language. Three languages only.
entries.ideas_for_us: Some sign-level statistics transfer across unrelated languages that share a script, others do not. In the logo-syllabic arm, test logograms borrowed from another language (as in Hittite) as a separate kind of mismatch. Their Elamite resources may feed the Elamite bridge.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Relevant to the logo-syllabic axis: a 34.7% share of foreign logograms broke the sign-statistics method. Consider adding 'foreign logograms' as a variant in the logogram-share slice; no change to sealed stage 1.

entries.title: Radiocarbon-Inferred Population Trajectories for Southeastern Arabia During the Bronze Age
entries.question: How did population in Bronze Age Oman and the UAE rise and fall?
entries.tried: Summed radiocarbon modelling with two Bayesian methods.
entries.method_data: 1280 radiocarbon dates across Arabia; 288 from the Southeast (Oman and UAE), 3200-1300 cal BC.
entries.key_results: Growth until the mid-Early Bronze Age, decline before the end of the 3rd millennium, growth to a Middle Bronze Age peak, then significant decline in the Late Bronze Age. The two models disagree on magnitude.
entries.limits: Abstract only; radiocarbon density is a rough proxy for population.
entries.ideas_for_us: A dated activity curve for Magan, the Indus trade partner. Compare with dated Indus-sign finds in the Gulf to see whether Indus-script presence tracks Magan's late 3rd-millennium dip.

entries.title: Towards Ancient Meroitic Decipherment: A Computational Approach
entries.question: Can embeddings and cross-lingual alignment with Late Egyptian (a contact language, not a relative) help read Meroitic vocabulary?
entries.tried: Build the first machine-readable Meroitic corpus, train word2vec, and align to Late Egyptian with VecMap unsupervised, anchored on numerals, or anchored on a noun dictionary.
entries.method_data: 871 Meroitic texts or phrases (augmented by swapping names); 302 Late Egyptian texts (1,729 types, 99,338 tokens); seven small evaluation dictionaries. French-English with a 26-pair seed as a skyline.
entries.key_results: No alignment setting induced a lexicon on an unseen dictionary. The best setting, numeral-anchored with 100-dimension vectors, stayed at or below 20% even on its training dictionary. The authors call the results abysmal and blame data scarcity and spelling variation.
entries.limits: Tiny corpus; Egyptian is unrelated to Meroitic; word-level only. Closer relatives (Nubian, Nara) not yet usable as corpora.
entries.ideas_for_us: A real-world far-mismatch case where a handful of anchors (numerals) did not lift recovery at small size. Their open corpus (github Joshua-Otten/Meroitic-Corpus) is a candidate extra retrodiction target with known sign values but partly unknown vocabulary.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Consistent with the claim that anchors cannot rescue a far-mismatch model at small size; one data point, not a test. No change.

entries.title: Indus Signs and Graffiti Marks of Tamil Nadu: A Morphological Study
entries.venue: Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology
entries.question: Most pottery marks from 140 Tamil Nadu sites have a similar-looking Indus sign.
entries.tried: The Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology documented graffiti-bearing potsherds from sites across the state as part of a project to document and digitise graffiti and Tamil-Brahmi sherds (p. 29).
entries.method_data: Rajan and Sivanantham sorted the documented marks by shape into base signs, variants (a base sign with extra strokes) and composites (more than one base sign) (p. 29, Table 4 on p. 33). They compared these shapes with Indus signs from Mahadevan's 1977 list and with graffiti on Indus pottery, and illustrated the matches in 100 plates (pp. 35-37). They set the comparison within a wider argument that new AMS and OSL dates make the South Indian Iron Age contemporary with the Indus Copper Age (pp. 23, 27-28). They describe the study as morphological, not linguistic (p. 37).
entries.key_results: 15,184 graffiti-bearing sherds have been reported from 140 sites in Tamil Nadu, and nearly 14,165 were documented (p. 29, Table 3). Nearly 2,107 signs were classed into 42 base signs, 544 variants and 1,521 composites (p. 29; Table 4, p. 33). Of the 42 base signs and their variants, nearly 60% have parallels in the Indus script, and more than 90% of South Indian graffiti marks have parallels among Indus graffiti marks (p. 35). They list 27 Tamil Nadu signs with 'exact parallels' and give 22 matching Mahadevan sign numbers, including 86, 125, 162, 176, 204, 328 and 365 (p. 35 and footnote 1). They note differences as well: sign 1.0 faces all directions in Tamil Nadu, mostly up, but always faces right on Indus sealings and left on seals; sign 3.0 is absent from Indus seals but present in Indus graffiti; sign 9.0 stands alone in Indus and South Indian graffiti but goes with vertical lines on Indus seals (pp. 35-36). About 70% of graffiti marks and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions are on black-and-red ware (p. 23). The early iron dates they tabulate include calibrated ages of 1030 to 1569 BCE in the first rows of Table 2 (p. 27); the foreword says the dates push iron in South India to the mid-3rd millennium BCE (p. 11). They call the research embryonic because of limited data (p. 35) and say more cultural items are needed to prove contact (p. 38).
entries.limits: This is the largest systematic catalogue of South Indian graffiti marks, with a published base-sign scheme and site counts, which makes testing possible. The 'parallel' judgements are visual and made by the authors, with no rule for what counts as a match and no chance rate; simple shapes such as circles, crosses, arrows and ladders will match across many unrelated mark systems. The comparison mixes Indus seal signs with Indus pottery graffiti, so a 90% match to Indus graffiti says little about the script on seals. The sections read give no dates for the individual sherds compared; the contemporaneity argument rests on iron and pottery dates, not on dated graffiti. The project already found that look-alike marks do not behave like the Indus signs they resemble (atlas 8.3), though that test was not preregistered.
entries.ideas_for_us: We tested whether look-alikes behave alike. They do not, so this route is closed for now. Measure the chance rate of 'parallels': apply a fixed shape-matching rule to the 42 base signs and to control mark sets (random stroke figures of matched complexity, and potters' marks from an unrelated tradition), and count how often each finds a match in Mahadevan's 417 signs. (The 60% and 90% figures have no baseline; if random simple marks also reach 50-60%, the parallels carry no signal.) Preregister and rerun the 'look-alikes behave alike' test with the new base-sign scheme: for each of the 22 Mahadevan signs the book pairs with a Tamil Nadu sign, compare position in composites (first, last, alone) with position in Indus texts against a shuffled pairing. (The book itself notes positional claims (sign 16.0 and 23.0 mostly at the start of composites); atlas 8.3 found p = 0.51 but had no preregistration and used an older mapping.)
entries.read_note: full text (the 145-page 2025 book 'Indus Signs and Graffiti Marks of Tamil Nadu: A Morphological Study' by K. Rajan and R. Sivanantham, free on tamildigitallibrary.in; the text pages were read and the 100 plates were not inspected image by image; tngraffiti.in itself was not opened because the project found it behind a Cloudflare challenge; the 2026 'Inscribed Potsherds' volumes were already read by the project in experiments/tn_brahmi_graffiti and were not reread)

entries.title: Novel 4400-year-old ancestral component in a tribe speaking a Dravidian language
entries.authors: Sequeira JJ, Krishna MS, van Driem G, Mustak MS, Das R
entries.question: Do Dravidian-speaking groups such as the Koraga carry a distinct ancestry that could mark Proto-Dravidian speakers?
entries.tried: Genotype Koraga individuals and model their ancestry against Indian and ancient references.
entries.method_data: Koraga samples on the Infinium Global Screening Array; PCA and admixture modelling (read from the 2024 bioRxiv preprint version).
entries.key_results: Proposes a fourth ancestry source, called 'Proto-Dravidian', branching from a basal Middle Eastern component, with a plausible origin not later than 4,400 years ago between the Iranian plateau and the Indus valley. Says most non-tribal South Asians still carry it.
entries.limits: Read the preprint, not the final version. Labelling a genetic component 'Proto-Dravidian' assumes a gene-language link. Co-author van Driem holds a particular Elamo-Dravidian view. Array data, one tribe.
entries.ideas_for_us: Bears on the mismatch study as a weak prior for a Dravidian-type language near the Indus by about 4,400 years ago. Use only as context; our language-model test should not depend on it.

entries.title: River drought forcing of the Harappan metamorphosis
entries.authors: Solanki H, Jain V, Thirumalai K, Rajagopalan B, Mishra VK
entries.question: How often and how badly did droughts hit Indus rivers between the Mature and Late Harappan?
entries.tried: Combine paleoclimate records with transient climate simulations and a hydrological model.
entries.method_data: Three transient simulations (TraCE-21ka, MPI, TR6AV) checked against Sahiya cave speleothem and lake records; VIC hydrological model for river discharge; SPI drought metrics.
entries.key_results: Four severe droughts (>85 years each): D1 4445-4358, D2 4122-4021, D3 3826-3663, D4 3531-3418 yr BP. D1 hit 65% of the IVC region with ~5% less rainfall and lasted ~88 years. D3 was worst: ~164 years, ~13% less rainfall, >91% of the region. D2 coincides with the 4.2 ka event; Ganweriwala and Kalibangan regions were less affected in D2.
entries.limits: Model-based; simulations differ in regional rainfall. Sahiya validation R2 = 0.46. Authors note social and economic factors also mattered.
entries.ideas_for_us: Gives dated drought windows. If inscriptions can be phased, test whether sign repertoire or inscription frequency changes across D1-D4 boundaries by region (e.g. central Indus vs Ghaggar).

entries.title: A Systematic Review of Computational Approaches to Deciphering Bronze Age Aegean and Cypriot Scripts
entries.question: What has computation achieved on Linear A, Linear B, Cypro-Minoan and related scripts?
entries.tried: Systematic review.
entries.method_data: Review of published computational work.
entries.key_results: Restates Gelb and Whiting: an unknown script writing an unknown language might be undecipherable. Reports no quantitative decipherability analysis.
entries.limits: Review; skimmed sections 2, 4 and 8.
entries.ideas_for_us: Cite it to show the gap the mismatch study fills: nobody has measured decipherability.

entries.title: Cretan Hieroglyphic (introduction and chapter 1)
entries.question: How does Cretan Hieroglyphic work on seals versus clay?
entries.tried: Repeated sign groups on seals are formulae tied to roles.
entries.method_data: Edited volume; corpus survey.
entries.key_results: Repeated sign groups make up almost half of the material on seals but are rare on clay.
entries.limits: Partial read (introduction, sections 1.1-1.4).
entries.ideas_for_us: Test face specialisation on multi-face Indus objects: one formula face plus unique faces (survey idea 3).

entries.title: Decipherment-Aware Multilingual Learning in Jointly Trained Language Models
entries.question: Is unsupervised cross-lingual learning in jointly trained models (like mBERT) a decipherment process, and what limits it?
entries.tried: Build nine bilingual 'decipherment' settings (English vs. ciphered English with different domain, word order and tokenisation), and relate cross-lingual performance to corpus divergence.
entries.method_data: Controlled English-to-fake-English settings; divergence measured by Jensen-Shannon on unigrams and by cross-perplexity of a source-trained model on target text; bilingual lexicon induction and retrieval as outputs; an added dictionary-alignment loss as an anchor.
entries.key_results: Lexicon induction falls as source-target divergence rises (shown in figures, no table values quoted here). The paper links the ceiling to Shannon's key equivocation: the key entropy never reaches zero, so unsupervised lexicon induction has an upper bound. A small bilingual dictionary added as an alignment loss lifts retrieval and translation past that bound.
entries.limits: Synthetic English-only pairs; the metric is lexicon induction, not sign values. Figures only; few exact numbers. Header dated 2021 though posted 2024.
entries.ideas_for_us: Their cross-perplexity divergence is close to our excess cross-entropy; cite it as precedent for a perplexity-based mismatch axis. Their dictionary-alignment step is an anchor mechanism to compare with our fixed-sign anchors.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Prior qualitative evidence for a divergence-set ceiling that anchors (a dictionary) lift. It narrows the novelty of the claim 'mismatch sets a ceiling, anchors lift it' and should be cited; our quantitative boundary and exchange rate remain new.

entries.title: Disambiguating numeral sequences to decipher ancient accounting corpora
entries.question: Which number system does each proto-Elamite numeral sequence belong to?
entries.tried: Bootstrapped classifiers plus checks of totals can assign numerals to number systems.
entries.method_data: Proto-Elamite tablets; classifiers; arithmetic consistency of totals.
entries.key_results: M288 entries are always exactly 4 times an adjacent M376 entry and 2 times an adjacent M367~i entry (44 entries).
entries.limits: Depends on tablets with totals, which the Indus corpus lacks.
entries.ideas_for_us: Test for a characteristic magnitude per counted Indus sign, out of sample (survey idea 5).

entries.title: Historical Language Models in Cryptanalysis: Case Studies on English and German
entries.authors: Megyesi, Sikora, Fornmark, Waldispühl, Kopal and Mikhalev
entries.question: Does decipherment of historical homophonic ciphers improve when the language model comes from the same century as the cipher, rather than from modern text?
entries.tried: Attack synthetic homophonic ciphers built from dated English and German texts with n-gram models from each century, a merged historical model and a modern Gutenberg model.
entries.method_data: HistCorp and other dated corpora (14th to 20th century); 3-, 4- and 5-gram models; ciphertexts of 200 and 500 characters; hill climbing and simulated annealing in CrypTool 2. A model scores a point if it reaches accuracy of at least 80%.
entries.key_results: Century-specific historical models do best on texts from the 17th century or earlier (English) and before the 19th century (German). 5-gram models do best on more modern texts and 4-gram on older ones; on 200-character texts 5-grams beat 3- and 4-grams. Longer ciphertexts give higher accuracy. The large modern Gutenberg model beats the merged historical model in most German cases.
entries.limits: Results are counts of solved texts per model (figures), not accuracy curves against a divergence measure. Two languages, two lengths. Alphabetic only.
entries.ideas_for_us: Diachronic distance within one language is a natural mismatch ladder with exact ground truth (same script, dated texts). Add a 'same language, different century' pair to the training set. Check whether model order interacts with size under mismatch, since they found shorter texts favour higher-order models.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: Supports the premise (model mismatch lowers recovery at fixed length) with a temporal, not genetic, mismatch. Suggests adding a diachronic pair; does not require changing the sealed stages.

entries.title: Sequence models for document structure identification in an undeciphered script
entries.question: Can unsupervised models find the "header" signs of proto-Elamite tablets?
entries.tried: Header signs occupy a distinct slot that a sequence model can find without labels.
entries.method_data: HMMs and Transformer attention on the proto-Elamite corpus, scored against expert header labels.
entries.key_results: An HMM state found only at text start matches expert labels at precision 0.93 and recall 0.67. A regression on Transformer attention to pre-numeral signs gets 92% against a 77% majority baseline.
entries.limits: Proto-Elamite is an accounting corpus with numerals throughout; Indus texts are much shorter.
entries.ideas_for_us: Port the slot-localised design to Indus: test whether the terminal or the initial slot carries the object-type signal (survey idea 1).

entries.title: Unsupervised deep learning supports reclassification of Bronze age Cypriot writing system
entries.question: Images plus context sorted Cypro-Minoan’s variant shapes into signs.
entries.tried: Corazza, Tamburini, Valério and Ferrara built an image dataset of Cypro-Minoan signs cropped from the published drawings, each labelled by inscription, position and published reading.
entries.method_data: They trained DeepCluster-v2, an unsupervised image clustering network, and a context-aware version they call Sign2Vec-d that also learns to predict, from the left and right neighbour images, whether the middle sign is a word divider. They trained 20 copies of each model from different random starts and concatenated the outputs into one 2,560-dimension vector per sign image. They computed a 'paleographic vector': the average shift from a sign's shape on non-tablet objects to its shape on clay tablets, learned from signs everyone agrees on. They then applied that vector to disputed signs found only on one kind of object, to see whether it points to a proposed variant on the other kind, with a leave-one-out check and binomial nulls.
entries.key_results: The dataset holds 2,899 usable sign images from 213 inscriptions, after removing 600 damaged or excluded images from a start of 3,499 (Materials, The dataset). In the embedding, signs from clay tablets sit at the periphery and signs from other objects at the core; this tracks writing medium more than the traditional CM1/CM2/CM3 split (Results, Fig. 6). Single clusters often did not match graphemes; instead each grapheme formed a 'filament' running from core to periphery (Results). On 32 agreed graphemes, the leave-one-out paleographic vector found the right tablet form first for 69% with Sign2Vec-d (top-2 81%) and 66% with DeepCluster-v2 (Table 3). On 13 proposed merges of signs in complementary distribution it scored 8/13 top-1 and 9/13 top-2 (Poisson binomial p = 1.0e-7), and on 3 more merges 2/3 (p = 1.7e-3) (Results, S7-S8 Tables). The model also flagged 27 sign images whose published labels looked wrong; tests relabelled 26 (DeepCluster-v2) and 20 (Sign2Vec-d) of 31 cases (Results, Preliminary relabelling). They conclude Cypro-Minoan is one script whose signs vary by medium, not three scripts (Conclusions).
entries.limits: The key validation is sound in design: the vector is learned on agreed signs and tested on held-out signs, with an explicit chance rate. The chance rate (1 in 64) is generous to the model because it ignores that frequent signs and similar shapes are easier to match. The context part of the model relies on word dividers, which are 57% of Cypro-Minoan trigrams; Indus has no dividers, so that part does not transfer. Drawings, not photographs, were used, so the editors' own choices are baked into the images.
entries.ideas_for_us: We tried it on two older scripts whose sign lists are known. Shape plus context merged too many signs that are not the same, and context alone was almost always wrong. Shape alone did best. On the Indus texts, a shape-only list fits unseen texts a little better than the 400-sign list, but a second team found half of that gain is one choice (three fish shapes counted as one sign) and it did not repeat on texts found after 1977. So the texts do not settle the count. The 700 side cannot be tested at all: most of those extra signs appear once or twice. Build an Indus 'medium vector': learn the average shape shift between carved seal forms and incised or moulded tablet and pot forms from agreed signs, then test whether Wells signs that are split from a Mahadevan sign and are restricted to one medium land on their partner. (The project tried shape plus context and shape alone, but not the medium-shift idea that worked best for Cypro-Minoan; many Wells splits may be the same sign carved versus scratched.) Use the leave-one-out validation design itself: on proto-cuneiform and Proto-Elamite, learn a variant-shift vector from known allograph pairs and score held-out pairs at top-1, as a known-answer bar before any Indus run. (This gives a cleaner known-answer test than the merge-precision bar used in signlist_shape, and it is cheap with the glyph sets already on disk.)
entries.read_note: full text

entries.title: Can Sequence-to-Sequence Models Crack Substitution Ciphers?
entries.question: Can one multilingual sequence model decipher ciphers without knowing the language?
entries.tried: Train on many languages at once, without language ID.
entries.method_data: Ciphers in 14 languages; the Borg cipher.
entries.key_results: Adding training languages lowers performance. The Borg cipher is cracked using a Latin model.
entries.limits: No held-out related-language test; no size by mismatch analysis.
entries.ideas_for_us: Pooled-language training as a way to reduce mismatch: compare with a pooled related-language model in our study.

entries.title: Compositionality of complex graphemes in the undeciphered Proto-Elamite script (with Born et al. 2019 and Monroe et al. 2025)
entries.question: Without knowing the language, they found which signs head an entry, which are built from parts, and which number system each count uses.
entries.tried: Born et al. 2021 trained image-aware BiLSTM language models on the proto-Elamite corpus to test whether complex signs are built from simpler ones.
entries.method_data: They tested whether a complex sign's embedding is close to the sum of its parts and measured a pairing consistency score for inner and outer components. Born 2019 used hierarchical clustering, n-grams and LDA topic models to find structure in proto-Elamite tablets. Born 2023 disambiguated numeral systems from summation structure with a bootstrapped classifier and cautious rule selection.
entries.key_results: The corpus has 1,399 tablets, 33,778 tokens, 7,508 broken tokens, 11,364 numerals, 14,906 non-numeric signs and 1,107 complex-grapheme tokens (Born 2021, data section). In the additive test at k = 15, the image-aware model with 64 dimensions finds 61 compositional complex graphemes (Born 2021, Table 2). The pairing consistency score is 0.760 for inner and 0.536 for outer components, so inner signs specialise the outer sign (Born 2021, Table 4). Containment forms a strict hierarchy: no two signs contain each other (Born 2021, Figure 2). The authors warn that conventional sign names act as distractors and suggest relabelling signs from context and shape (Born 2021, discussion). Born 2019 reports that perplexity drops above 80 topics and coherence peaks near 110 (conclusion). Born 2023 finds correlations between tablet content and numeral magnitude, evaluated only on a hand-disambiguated subset (conclusion).
entries.limits: Proto-Elamite is a close methodological cousin of Indus: undeciphered, with complex signs and numerals, and these papers release code (github.com/sfu-natlang/pe-compositionality). Proto-Elamite tablets are long administrative texts with numerals, so methods may lose power on short Indus seals. The NEA 2025 synthesis was not reachable, so this record does not cover its claims.
entries.ideas_for_us: We tried the pieces that fit. Indus signs that look like Proto-Elamite or proto-cuneiform signs do not behave like them (0 of 5 tests), complex signs do not split into their parts, and no known number system matches the Indus counts. Still untried: letting a model find genres from scratch. Test whether Indus framed and compound signs form a strict containment hierarchy: list every 'sign inside or attached to sign' relation in M77 and check for cycles against a random-pairing null. (An acyclic hierarchy is a structural fact that both writing and emblem systems might show, but it is untested for Indus and is distinct from the closed ligature-decomposition route.) Compute a pairing consistency score for Indus compounds: does the inner or attached element vary with the base sign's contexts more than the base varies with the element's? (Born 2021 found inner elements specialise the outer sign; the same asymmetry in Indus would say which component carries the modifying role.)
entries.read_note: partial (Born et al. 2021 ACL Findings paper read in full; Born 2019 and Born 2023 abstracts and conclusions read; the 2025 Near Eastern Archaeology article, doi 10.1086/738240, returned 403 at the publisher and was not read)

entries.title: Killing the Priest-King: Addressing Egalitarianism in the Indus Civilization
entries.question: Did the Indus have a ruling class?
entries.tried: Review of a century of evidence on Indus inequality.
entries.method_data: Literature synthesis.
entries.key_results: No clear evidence for elite tombs, palaces or big temples; argues a ruling class is not required for social complexity.
entries.limits: Abstract only; interpretive.
entries.ideas_for_us: If there was no king, seal texts may name offices, guilds or households rather than rulers. Frame administrative-reading hypotheses accordingly.

entries.title: Bronze Age weight systems as a measure of market integration in Western Eurasia
entries.authors: Ialongo N, Hermann R, Rahmstorf L
entries.question: How did weight systems spread and diverge across Bronze Age Western Eurasia?
entries.tried: Compare statistical error of early weight units; replica-weight experiments; simulate drift from one original unit.
entries.method_data: Archaeological weight units from Mesopotamia to Europe; replica-weight error tests; propagation-of-error simulation.
entries.key_results: Errors of early units overlap between Mesopotamia and Europe; simulated random drift reproduces the observed units; the earliest systems do not need strong state intervention.
entries.limits: Abstract only; Indus weights are a separate system and their role in this model was not checked here.
entries.ideas_for_us: Same logic can test whether Indus weights (and Gulf finds of Indus-standard weights) fit a merchant-driven model. Pair weight findspots with inscription findspots.

entries.title: The Indus script and economics: a role for Indus seals and tablets in rationing and administration of labor
entries.question: What economic job did seals and tablets do?
entries.tried: Miniature tablets were ration tokens and human-figure signs are labour categories.
entries.method_data: Argument from the 1997 Harappa miniature tablets and patterned texts.
entries.key_results: Proposes reading patterned texts as Prefix = institution, Medial = quantity, Core = commodity, Terminal = function of the sealing or tablet.
entries.limits: Interpretive; no statistical test.
entries.ideas_for_us: Test whether human-figure signs follow numerals more than matched signs (survey idea 2).

entries.title: Deciphering Related Languages
entries.question: Can one related language be converted into another with no parallel data, as a character cipher?
entries.tried: Character-level decipherment between related language pairs.
entries.method_data: Six pairs, e.g. Bosnian/Serbian, Macedonian/Bulgarian, Danish/Swedish.
entries.key_results: Best BLEU4: Bosnian to Serbian 39.9, Macedonian to Bulgarian 11.9, Malay to Indonesian 10.4, Danish to Swedish 6.9, Afrikaans to Dutch 4.3, Belarusian to Polish 1.9.
entries.limits: Translation, not script decipherment; no size curve or anchors.
entries.ideas_for_us: Success varies widely among close pairs, so a single 'related' label is not enough. Supports measuring mismatch per pair (ΔH) rather than by family.

entries.title: Decoding Anagrammed Texts Written in an Unknown Language and Script
entries.question: Can the plaintext language of a cipher be identified among hundreds of languages?
entries.tried: Trial decipherment against each candidate language.
entries.method_data: Ciphers across 380 languages; the Voynich manuscript.
entries.key_results: Trial decipherment identifies the language 97.1% of the time on test data. Of 11 errors, 7 involve closely related languages such as Serbian and Bosnian.
entries.limits: No measurement of recovery when only the related language is available.
entries.ideas_for_us: Related languages are confusable under the objective, so a 'best language' result for Indus means little without wrong-language nulls.

entries.title: Evidence for Patterns of Selective Urban Migration in the Greater Indus Valley (2600-1900 BC): A Lead and Strontium Isotope Mortuary Analysis
entries.authors: Valentine B, Kamenov GD, Kenoyer JM, Shinde V, Mushrif-Tripathy V, Otarola-Castillo E, Krigbaum J
entries.question: Were people buried in Harappan cemeteries locals or migrants?
entries.tried: Sr and Pb isotopes along tooth development sequences.
entries.method_data: Harappa: 44 teeth, MNI 38; Farmana: 33 teeth from 17 individuals; local baselines from fauna (Harappa n = 13, Rakhigarhi n = 8, Farmana n = 3) and sediments.
entries.key_results: Early-forming teeth are non-local and later teeth local, consistent with childhood migration from hinterlands. Cemetery populations were almost entirely first-generation immigrants, so burial may mark a regulated migration institution.
entries.limits: Small samples; non-local Pb could come from imported goods; Harappa burials often disturbed.
entries.ideas_for_us: If urban cemeteries hold migrants, cities mixed speakers from different hinterlands. That favours testing for multilingual or non-phonetic layers in the script, and region-specific sign sets.

entries.title: Decipherment Complexity in 1:1 Substitution Ciphers
entries.question: How hard is optimal decipherment as a search problem?
entries.tried: Reduce bigram-model decipherment to a known hard problem.
entries.method_data: Theory: equivalence to the quadratic assignment problem.
entries.key_results: Optimal decipherment under a bigram model is NP-hard; the unigram case is a linear sum assignment and solvable.
entries.limits: Computational, not statistical, hardness. No experiments, no mismatch.
entries.ideas_for_us: Supports the study's split between computational failure (search) and statistical failure (the objective prefers wrong keys).

entries.title: Large Scale Decipherment for Out-of-Domain Machine Translation
entries.question: Does word decipherment scale to large data when the model comes from a different domain?
entries.tried: Train the model on a different chronological half of Gigaword (mild mismatch).
entries.method_data: Gigaword word cipher; Transtac.
entries.key_results: Accuracy reaches 92.2%, and accuracy rises as more data is added. Transtac improves from 82.5% to 88.1%.
entries.limits: Mild domain mismatch only.
entries.ideas_for_us: Under mild mismatch accuracy keeps rising with data. Use it to place where the regime changes from 'more data helps' to a plateau, and compare with our genre pairs.

entries.title: Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization
entries.authors: Giosan L, Clift PD, Macklin MG, Fuller DQ, et al.
entries.question: How did rivers and monsoon change around Harappan urbanism and decline?
entries.tried: Geomorphic mapping and dating of Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra landscapes.
entries.method_data: Morphology and chronology of Punjab rivers and the Indus mega-ridge in Sindh.
entries.key_results: Urbanism flourished for about 600 years; from about 3,900 years ago settlement shrank and shifted east. Rivers stabilised as aridity grew after about 5,000 BP. Only monsoon-fed rivers were active on the Ghaggar interfluve in the Holocene, not a glacier-fed 'Sarasvati'.
entries.limits: Abstract only; later work (e.g. Shekhar 2026) argues the opposite on perennial flow.
entries.ideas_for_us: Standard reference for the eastward shift; use as the baseline model for region-by-period inscription comparisons.

entries.title: Simple Effective Decipherment via Combinatorial Optimization
entries.question: Can lexicon matching be solved well by plain combinatorial optimisation?
entries.tried: Treat decipherment of cognate lexicons as a matching problem.
entries.method_data: Romance cognate lexicons; Ugaritic/Hebrew lexicons restricted to cognates.
entries.key_results: Romance reaches 90.1%. Ugaritic/Hebrew restricted to cognates reaches 90.4%, with 28 of 33 alphabet entries correct.
entries.limits: No mismatch gradient, size curve or anchors. Restricting to cognates makes the task easier.
entries.ideas_for_us: A cheap baseline to include in stage-5 retrodiction for Ugaritic.

entries.title: Deciphering Foreign Language
entries.question: Can a foreign language be translated with monolingual data only, treating it as a cipher?
entries.tried: Word-substitution decipherment with Bayesian inference.
entries.method_data: Temporal expressions, Transtac, and Spanish-to-English MT with English monolingual data.
entries.key_results: Transtac: 60.1% at 9k tokens and 80.0% at 100k with a 2-gram model, 82.5% with a 3-gram. Spanish-to-English BLEU 48.7 on the Time set against 88.0 for MOSES. Scores improve little beyond 10,000 training sentences.
entries.limits: Not a script task; no controlled mismatch.
entries.ideas_for_us: Another plateau-with-size data point under cross-language decipherment.

entries.title: Statistical analysis of the Indus script using n-grams
entries.authors: Yadav, Joglekar, Rao, Vahia, Mahadevan and Adhikari
entries.question: What do n-gram models reveal about the structure of the Indus texts?
entries.tried: Fit Markov n-gram models to the Mahadevan concordance.
entries.method_data: Mahadevan 1977 corpus; n-gram models; restoration of missing signs.
entries.key_results: The abstract says the analysis cannot conclusively establish that the script encodes natural language.
entries.limits: Structure only; no language model of a candidate language.
entries.ideas_for_us: The baseline n-gram model our restoration and mismatch work build on.

entries.title: Historical Implications of a Pattern of Dates at Piedras Negras, Guatemala
entries.question: She matched glyph patterns to the lifespans of rulers, and found births and accessions without sounding anything out.
entries.tried: Proskouriakoff sorted the dated inscriptions of Piedras Negras into sets, each carved on a group of consecutive monuments that starts with a stela showing the 'ascension motif' (abstract).
entries.method_data: In each set she marked the earliest date, tagged by the 'upended frog' glyph, and a date in the first dedicatory hotun tagged by the 'toothache' glyph (abstract). She compared the intervals between these dates with a human lifetime (abstract; quoted from p. 460 in Callaway 2014). She then looked at the glyphs that follow the action glyphs and compared them with the figures shown on the monuments, including Yaxchilan lintels (abstract). The abstract describes no phonetic readings; the argument rests on dates, glyph positions and pictures.
entries.key_results: No single series exceeds a reasonable lifetime; the distance between the initial date of a series and the inaugural dates of the next does not exceed a normal lifetime (abstract; p. 460 as quoted in Callaway 2014). She proposed that the initial date is a birth or name day, the inaugural date an accession, and each set the history of one reign (abstract). Variants of the upended frog and toothache glyphs suggest they are verbal action glyphs (abstract). Groups of glyphs after the action glyph are names and titles, and they contain a female head prefix when they refer to robed or skirted figures (abstract). Initial and inaugural dates were identified at other sites by the same glyphs, but no connected series of reigns was found outside Piedras Negras (abstract). Lunar and 'determinant' meanings given to the dates had no relation to the action glyphs beside them (abstract).
entries.limits: The method works without sounds because it pairs recurring glyphs with an independent, exactly known variable: calendar dates. It also used a second independent variable, the figures carved on the same monument, which is how the female prefix was found. The Indus texts have no dates and very few pictures of people beside text, so the method cannot be copied directly. Only the abstract and a secondary account were read, so the paper's tables and exact intervals are not reported here.
entries.ideas_for_us: We tested it on the 1930s excavation registers. Seals found in streets carry the same signs as seals found in rooms, and broken seals carry the same signs as pieces of whole ones. Most other fates, such as burnt, buried or hoarded seals, are recorded too rarely to test. One small lead, that damaged seals keep more end signs, did not survive a second team: it came from damaged seals having shorter texts. Use a lifetime bound as the independent variable: for identical seal texts found at more than one stratigraphic depth at one site, test whether their depth spread is smaller than for random pairs of seals, as personal seals should be, or as wide as office or commodity labels. (It is the closest Indus analogue to her lifetime test; local_repeats (atlas 10b.9) could not test office seals because it found only one dated pair, so this needs new dated data rather than a new method.) Copy her figure test: on objects that show human figures beside a text, check whether a sign group changes with a figure attribute (horned headdress, bangles, skirt or posture), as her female prefix did. (It uses the only independent 'picture' variable Indus objects offer, and it is not the same question as scene_text, which looked for a vessel sign on offering scenes.)
entries.read_note: abstract only (the article in American Antiquity 25(4) is not open access: the doi.org link goes to JSTOR and the Cambridge Core PDF link redirected to the abstract page; the abstract was read there; I also read an open secondary source, Callaway 2014 in the PARI Journal, which quotes p. 460 of the paper and prints Thompson's 1958 letter about it)

entries.title: Beyond the Monumental: A Bronze Age Combustion Installation and Domestic Practices at Site S27, Failaka Island (Kuwait)
entries.question: What did daily life look like on Dilmun-period Failaka outside the big F3/F6 complexes?
entries.tried: Excavate and analyse a domestic combustion installation and its finds.
entries.method_data: Architecture, ceramics, and pollen from an intact vessel (SU19) in the combustion chamber at S27.
entries.key_results: Pollen of rice (Oryza) and olive in the vessel may indicate food preparation and links to wider exchange in the early 2nd millennium BCE.
entries.limits: Abstract only. Pollen of rice is not proof of rice trade.
entries.ideas_for_us: Failaka has Gulf-type seals with Indus signs. Domestic contexts like S27 could yield seals with secure context; watch for finds to add to the foreign corpus.

entries.title: Attention-Augmented LSTMs for Automatic Homophonic Ciphertext Decipherment
entries.question: Can a supervised attention LSTM decrypt homophonic ciphers whose keys come from a shared, known code pool?
entries.tried: Train on aligned ciphertext-plaintext pairs, without language models or search, and test on new keys from the same pool.
entries.method_data: Synthetic ciphers from English and Swedish texts dated 1500-1899 (ChronoFidelius); lengths 50-1,000; variable-length codes and simulated transcription errors.
entries.key_results: Near-perfect character accuracy for both languages and all periods, with reported F1 cells such as 0.982-0.993, and F1 for 50-character inputs stays at or near that level. The model fails predictably on ciphertexts outside the shared code pool.
entries.limits: Supervised; assumes the code pool is known, which is the opposite of an undeciphered script.
entries.ideas_for_us: Their 'known pool' setting is an extreme anchor regime; little direct use beyond showing that strong priors on the symbol set make length nearly irrelevant.

entries.title: Holocene North Asian gene flow and cryptic substructure in the genome history of Nilgiri tribes
entries.authors: Desai S, Tharu MK, Pandey PS, Welikala AHJ, Tamang R, Chaubey G
entries.question: What ancestry streams make up the Dravidian-speaking Toda, Kota and Kurumba of the Nilgiris?
entries.tried: Whole-genome and mitogenome analysis against a Eurasian reference panel.
entries.method_data: Whole genomes and complete mtDNA from Toda, Kota, Kurumba; PCA, ADMIXTURE, fineSTRUCTURE, qpWave, qpAdm with Onge-, Indus-Periphery- and Steppe-MLBA-related sources.
entries.key_results: Five genetic clusters need at least three ancestry streams. Toda has the highest Indus-Periphery-related ancestry (~59% in the text) and lowest Onge-related. mtDNA C4a2c1 is linked to North Asian lineages, arriving ~7 ka.
entries.limits: Preprint. 'Indus Periphery' is a proxy built from outlier individuals at Gonur and Shahr-i Sokhta, not from Harappan heartland genomes. Genetics does not tell us language.
entries.ideas_for_us: Shows Indus-Periphery-related ancestry is high in some South Dravidian-speaking groups, consistent with (not proof of) a Dravidian-Indus link. For the mismatch study: a weak prior only; do not weight language-family hypotheses on ancestry.

entries.title: Comparative Stature Estimation and Skeletal Robusticity in the Indus Valley Civilization Populations: Long Bone Evidence from Three Sites
entries.authors: Gautam M, Bhattacharya N, Chanu YN, Das S, Kotal M, Ghosh Roy A, Harashawaradhana
entries.question: How tall and how robust were people at Rupar, Kalibangan and Lothal, and do the sites differ?
entries.tried: Estimate stature from broken long bones using a two-step regression (fragment -> bone length -> stature).
entries.method_data: 46 adults (Rupar 15, Kalibangan 12, Lothal 19) held by the Anthropological Survey of India; fragments of humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia, fibula; Steele (1970) fragment equations then Trotter and Gleser (1952) 'Mongoloid' male equations; Robusticity and Circularity indices; Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests.
entries.key_results: Pooled weighted mean stature 189.3 +/- 20.5 cm (range 147.2-231.0). Site means: Rupar 196.9, Kalibangan 189.2, Lothal 186.0 cm; difference not significant (p = 0.21). Femoral robusticity higher at Lothal, not significant (p = 0.093).
entries.limits: The statures are implausible: the authors themselves cite earlier estimates of about 165-170 cm for Harappan males. Sex could not be assigned; male equations applied to everyone (they say females are overestimated by about 8-12 cm). Equations from a non-South Asian reference group. Small samples. Preprint.
entries.ideas_for_us: Mainly a caution: do not cite these statures as fact. The skeletal collection list (Rupar, Kalibangan, Lothal at AnSI Kolkata) could be a future source of site-level bioarchaeology covariates.

entries.title: Hexagon KH-9 Imagery using Sunspot: Monitoring At-Risk Heritage and Development Pressure in Haryana India (1915-2021)
entries.authors: Gerrits PJ, Klehm C, Cothren J, ... Petrie CA
entries.question: How fast are archaeological mounds in Haryana being lost to farming and building, and when did the damage happen?
entries.tried: Fill the gap between 1914-15 Survey of India maps and modern satellite data using declassified 1975 Hexagon spy-satellite photos.
entries.method_data: Six 1975 KH-9 frames georeferenced in Sunspot (20-25 ground control points each); land cover classified for 1914-15, 1975 and 2021 (ESA WorldCover) around 12 sites: Rakhigarhi, Masudpur I and VII, Lohari Ragho I, Bhirrana, Kunal, Burj Pirwala, Bhuna, Agroha, Sirsa, Ankaar, Bahola.
entries.key_results: Ground not classed as cropland fell from 35% of the observed area (1915) to 14% (1975) and 4% (2021). Built-up land within 1 km: Rakhigarhi 3.9% -> 19.5% -> 23.7%; Bhirrana 9.2% -> 11.7% -> 20.1%; Sirsa reached 75.1% by 2021. The Masudpur-Lohari Ragho rural Harappan cluster stays at or below 1% built-up; its threat is cropland. At Rakhigarhi most village growth predates 1975.
entries.limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Only 12 sites. Site locations and rasters withheld to protect sites (available on request). Classes from three different sources are harmonised but not cross-calibrated.
entries.ideas_for_us: Site visibility and destruction bias what survives to be excavated, including seals. We could add a 'site preservation / pressure class' covariate when comparing inscription counts per site in Haryana. The MAHSA database (close to 3,000 site locations in Haryana) is an open site list for findspot mapping.

entries.title: Read(?) the Signs: By Solving a Math-Puzzle or by Wearing Harappan Shoes?
entries.question: What does the push to 'decipher' the Indus signs (incl. the 2025 USD 1 million prize) miss from an archaeological view?
entries.tried: Historiography of decipherment prizes and debates since 2004; critique framed by Gero's 'honouring ambiguities'.
entries.method_data: Critical review; no new data.
entries.key_results: Argues that the focus on a 'readable' script works against archaeology's aims, and points out gaps in current studies with pointers forward.
entries.limits: Abstract only. Position paper.
entries.ideas_for_us: A useful critic's checklist: report context (findspot, object type, stratigraphy) alongside any sign-level claim, and state what result would count against our hypothesis.

entries.title: A Multi-Isotopic Approach to Examining Mobility and Social Reorganization During the Bronze Age Transition in Ras Al Khaimah, UAE
entries.question: Did people move during the Umm an-Nar to Wadi Suq transition at Shimal?
entries.tried: Sr, O and C isotopes in human teeth from tombs of both periods.
entries.method_data: 57 teeth from 50 individuals; two Umm an-Nar and four Wadi Suq tombs at Shimal.
entries.key_results: Sr ratios differ over time with only a slight Wadi Suq increase; O values differ between early tomb Unar 1 and all later tombs; C stable. Suggests continuity at an oasis plus some incomers seeking stability.
entries.limits: Abstract only.
entries.ideas_for_us: Context for the ~2000 BCE Gulf transition when Indus contact changes. Not directly testable on inscriptions.

entries.title: Bony labyrinth taxonomic identification and long-term evolution of livestock in the Southwest and Central Asia
entries.authors: Guignet A, Davoudi H, Hemelsdael A, et al.
entries.question: Can inner-ear bone shape identify sheep, goat and cattle and track domestication over 10,000 years?
entries.tried: Micro-CT and geometric morphometrics of the bony labyrinth.
entries.method_data: 78 modern reference specimens and 234 archaeological petrous bones from 51 sites across the Iranian Plateau, Central Asia, the Caucasus and the Indus Valley.
entries.key_results: Species-level identification for 228 of 234 specimens. Sheep, goats and cattle show contrasting, nonlinear size and shape trajectories over time.
entries.limits: Abstract only; Indus Valley share of the sample not seen.
entries.ideas_for_us: Background for animal motifs on seals (bull, zebu, goat). Not directly testable against the inscriptions.

entries.title: Bronze Age Trade Through River Networks: A Wharf Evidence from Naru Waro Dhoro, on the Indus Palaeochannel at Khairpur in Sindh, Pakistan
entries.authors: Hakal M, Ali M, Chang WA
entries.question: Was Naru Waro Dhoro a river port on an old Indus channel?
entries.tried: New field survey plus review of 1935 and 1955 excavations.
entries.method_data: Survey of cultural deposits over the palaeochannel bed; vegetation anomalies; comparison of old excavation finds.
entries.key_results: Thick cultural deposit directly over the old riverbed; a vegetation anomaly over about 600 ha on both sides of the channel; no permanent structures. Authors argue for wharf facilities and call it one of the largest commercial centres, especially in the regionalisation phase.
entries.limits: Abstract only. Wharf inferred from indirect clues; no architecture seen.
entries.ideas_for_us: Adds a candidate inland port to a findspot layer of trade nodes. Check if any inscribed objects are recorded from the site.

entries.title: AlphaOracle: Oracle bone script decipherment via human-workflow-inspired deep learning
entries.authors: Liu, Guan, Wang, Wang et al.
entries.question: Can a pipeline that follows the expert workflow (rubbing parsing, radical analysis, context retrieval, philological checks) help decipher oracle-bone characters?
entries.tried: A multi-stage system that outputs confidence-weighted evidence chains and reports for expert review.
entries.method_data: Digitized corpus of 73,883 rubbings, 45,364 scans and 23,755 studies; user study with 86 domain specialists.
entries.key_results: About 3,000 of 4,500 oracle-bone characters remain undeciphered. In the user study the system cut analysis time by 64%, and 79% of participants rated it highly useful. It proposes reading one character as a toponym or clan name.
entries.limits: Read at abstract and introduction depth. Agreement with experts is reported for selected test characters; depends on a known descendant script and huge corpus.
entries.ideas_for_us: Evidence-chain reports with confidence weights are a good format for presenting any Indus meaning-class claim to specialists.

entries.title: Building a Corpus and Database for Rare and Undeciphered Scripts
entries.authors: Megyesi, Rattenborg, Láng, Waldispühl and Héder
entries.question: How should a FAIR corpus and database for rare and undeciphered scripts be designed?
entries.tried: A unified data model for images, transliterations, transcriptions, annotations and metadata for low-resource and non-standard scripts (DESCRYPT programme).
entries.method_data: Design and workflow paper; examples include Indus, Rongorongo, Linear A and Proto-Elamite as target scripts.
entries.key_results: Describes the collection and digitisation workflow and database architecture; no evaluation numbers.
entries.limits: Design paper; data availability and licence not yet clear from what we read.
entries.ideas_for_us: A possible home or interchange format for our consensus Indus corpus; follow for released data.

entries.title: The Proportioned City: Ratio, Symbol, and Statecraft in the Metrological Foundations of the Indus Civilization
entries.question: Did the 4:2:1 Harappan brick ratio express a political and symbolic 'metrological order'?
entries.tried: Interpretive essay linking brick proportions, weights and town planning to ideology and governance.
entries.method_data: Narrative synthesis of secondary literature (mostly Kenoyer 1998); no new measurements, data or statistics.
entries.key_results: No new results. Argues the 4:2:1 brick was a 'metrological cosmogram' and that irregular Late Harappan bricks mark a 'semiotic dissolution'. Cites a brick-dimension variance of less than 3% across sites without primary data.
entries.limits: Low-bar journal. No data or methods. Some references could not be traced (e.g. an 'R. Jansen, Indus Urbanism and Material Rationality, ASI Press 2004'). Treat as opinion, not evidence.
entries.ideas_for_us: Little to use. If we want a brick-ratio covariate, measure it from primary excavation reports instead (e.g. brick sizes by phase at Harappa or Mohenjo-daro).

entries.title: Interpretable Oracle Bone Script Decipherment via Progressive Glyph Analysis with LVLMs
entries.authors: Peng, Zhao, Yu, Fu and Li
entries.question: Can a vision-language model map unseen oracle-bone glyphs to modern Chinese characters by first analysing radicals and pictographic form?
entries.tried: Train an LVLM in stages (radical analysis, pictographic analysis, then both) and use its written analysis to retrieve candidates from a dictionary.
entries.method_data: New PD-OBS dataset with radical and pictographic annotations; HUST-OBC and EVOBC benchmarks; 200 held-out deciphered character classes per dataset as the zero-shot test.
entries.key_results: Zero-shot Top-1 / Top-10: 16.8 / 53.7 on HUST-OBC and 33.3 / 64.1 on EVOBC. Commercial LVLMs (GPT-4.1, Qwen-VL-Max, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5) stay below 8% Top-1. The best diffusion baseline gives 18.3 / 27.5 and 30.4 / 50.5.
entries.limits: 'Unseen' means held-out deciphered characters, not truly undeciphered ones. Relies on a known descendant script, which the Indus script lacks.
entries.ideas_for_us: Shows the value of a descendant-script anchor for logograms; nothing comparable exists for Indus. Their held-out-deciphered protocol is a model for evaluating meaning-class proposals.

entries.title: Why change what works? Technological resilience in Harappan pottery from Bagasra (c. 2450-1900 BCE), Gujarat
entries.authors: Sarkar S, Boyatzis SC, Zacharias N, Ajithprasad P
entries.question: Did pottery making at Bagasra change through the 4.2 ka aridification?
entries.tried: Archaeometry plus chaine operatoire across the site's occupation.
entries.method_data: LED microscopy and pXRF on 73 sherds; SEM-EDS, FTIR, XRD on 17.
entries.key_results: Four clay paste groups; three stable through the ~500-year occupation. 15 of 17 samples fired at 800-900 C, two at 650-800 C.
entries.limits: Pilot study, small sample (authors say so).
entries.ideas_for_us: Continuity of craft through 4.2 ka at Bagasra (Gola Dhoro) argues against a sharp break there; if Bagasra has phased inscribed objects, check whether sign use also shows continuity.

entries.title: Reconstruction of lost Himalayan rivers: Climate change and anthropogenic interactions with reference to Sutlej-Ghaggar-Saraswati-Drishadvati, a mighty river basin
entries.question: What drove the evolution of the Ghaggar (Sarasvati) river system between the Sutlej and Yamuna?
entries.tried: Combine paleochannel mapping, sedimentology, satellite imagery, TL dating and borehole data.
entries.method_data: Paleochannel delineation; thermoluminescence dating; borehole logs in the Punjab-Haryana plains and near Delhi.
entries.key_results: A paleochannel about 1.5 km wide and over 40-50 m deep, with sediment ages of 5.3 +/- 0.6 ka; the modern Sutlej channel there seldom exceeds 150 m. Authors argue for a significant perennial river in the mid-Holocene, linked eastward toward the Yamuna near Delhi.
entries.limits: Abstract only. The perennial-river reading conflicts with Singh et al. 2017 (Sutlej left this course shortly after ~8 ka) and Giosan et al. 2012 (only monsoon-fed rivers in the Holocene). Treat as one side of an open debate.
entries.ideas_for_us: Keep both river models as alternative covariates. If seal-bearing sites along the Ghaggar cluster where a perennial channel is claimed, that would be a testable site-distribution pattern, not a script result.

entries.title: Dental microwear from the Harappan sites of Juna Khatiya and Rakhigarhi, India
entries.authors: Yhome RR, Rajesh SV, Rai N, Shinde VS, Abhayan GS, Conesa FC, Garcia-Granero JJ, Bhandari S, Tilva PP, Ungar PS
entries.question: Did urban Harappans eat softer, more processed food than earlier rural people?
entries.tried: Compare dental microwear texture between an Early Harappan cemetery and a Mature Harappan city.
entries.method_data: Dental microwear texture analysis; Juna Khatiya (Kutch, Early Harappan, n = 12) vs Rakhigarhi (Haryana, Mature Harappan, n = 10). SSRN preprint 10.2139/ssrn.5800208.
entries.key_results: (Not read: the abstract could not be opened; a search-engine summary is not evidence.) The more urban Rakhigarhi group shows lower microwear texture complexity, as predicted for more processed food. Authors note other factors also shape microwear.
entries.limits: Abstract-level only (from the SSRN listing); no complexity values or test statistics seen. Tiny samples; two sites differ in region as well as period.
entries.ideas_for_us: Minor for the script. Shows Juna Khatiya (Kutch) and Rakhigarhi skeletal series are available for site-level covariates.

entries.title: Decipherment of Indus Script: Current Status and Way Forward (seminar)
entries.question: A national meeting on the state of decipherment. No proceedings yet.
entries.tried: The Archaeological Survey of India announced a seminar on the decipherment of the Indus script and invited papers.
entries.method_data: The registration notice set a deadline of 30 June 2025 (notice 772).
entries.key_results: The concept note states that the script has over 400 principal signs and is hypothesised to be logo-syllabic (concept note). It says most scholars agree it was written right to left and that stroke signs are numerals (concept note). It names the lack of a bilingual text, the short texts and the small number of specimens as the main obstacles (concept note). It says the proceedings of the seminar are anticipated, but none were found online.
entries.limits: The note is a call for papers, not research, and gives no data or method. Without proceedings there is nothing to test yet.
entries.ideas_for_us: We have asked the agency whether readings proposed there can be scored on our open test bench. Offer a frozen hidden-sign test for any reading presented at the seminar: a proposer commits to sign values, we mask signs in held-out, family-clean texts, and the reading must predict them better than a trigram. (It gives claimed decipherments one shared, falsifiable score instead of case-by-case argument.) Test the concept note's consensus claims on M77: run the right-to-left direction check and the stroke-numeral check on family-clean texts and report how strong each is. (These are the shared starting points of most readings, so their strength should be measured, not assumed.)
entries.read_note: partial (the seminar concept note and registration notice; no proceedings or papers were found)

entries.title: Linguistic Predictability and Search Complexity: How Linguistic Redundancy Constraints the Landscape of Classical and Quantum Search
entries.question: How does the share of keys giving a plausible decryption (p_good) shrink with cipher length, and what does that imply for search cost?
entries.tried: Estimate p_good from 10,000 random permutations under character n-gram models of four Renaissance Italian works, and compare hill climbing, simulated annealing, QUBO annealing and Grover-style estimates.
entries.method_data: Machiavelli, Castiglione, Guicciardini and Ariosto; 25-letter historical orthography and the modern alphabet; cipher lengths 200-1000 characters.
entries.key_results: Score distributions narrow as length grows. p_good falls below 1e-4 for lengths of 600 or more at thresholds of 0.95 or above. The four texts give closely aligned curves despite genre differences. Grover estimates follow 1/sqrt(p_good).
entries.limits: Always uses the true language model; no mismatch. Monte-Carlo p_good estimates are noisy (non-monotone at 600).
entries.ideas_for_us: p_good under a mismatched model would measure how flat the landscape gets; it could explain the computational-failure regime. Note their genre curves align under the true model, while Korovina 2026 finds large cross-genre losses; the difference is model mismatch, which is our variable.
entries.bears_on_mismatch: No change; suggests an extra diagnostic (share of keys scoring above the truth key) for the statistical-vs-computational split.

entries.title: Deep Learning in Archiving Indus Script and Motif Information
entries.venue: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology 8(1)
entries.question: Image models that spot signs and animal motifs on photographs of seals.
entries.tried: The authors collected 1,004 seal images from the CISI volumes and Mahadevan 1977, leaving 963 after removing duplicates.
entries.method_data: They trained a YOLOv3 detector to find signs on 232 annotated images and tested it on 13. They trained a MobileNet classifier on 40 classes, 39 Mahadevan signs plus an 'Other' class, using 12,264 augmented crops. They also trained a motif classifier (MI-net) on 11 animal and field motifs.
entries.key_results: The sign classifier reaches 94.5% validation accuracy and an F1 score of 95% (results section). Five-fold cross-validation gives 85.28% accuracy (plus or minus 1.51) and F1 85.22% (plus or minus 1.53) (Table I). The final test used a class-balanced set of 200 unaugmented crops (results section). The motif classifier reaches a mean fold accuracy of 0.85 (results section).
entries.limits: Automatic sign reading from images could speed corpus building and check transcriptions. Only 40 classes are covered out of several hundred signs, and broken seals were excluded (section VI). The detector test set of 13 images is very small. The full datasets are available only on request, per the repository README.
entries.ideas_for_us: Reading signs straight from photos could settle the 1-in-8 disagreements between the two main transcriptions. We need open images first. Use a sign classifier's confusion matrix as an independent measure of which signs look alike, and check whether visually confusable pairs are also distributionally similar in M77. (It tests whether look-alike signs behave as allographs with a source of similarity that is not our own judgement. Our look-alike tests (atlas 8.1/8.2) used shape judgement; this would only add an outside measure, so it is low priority.) Score a sign detector's errors against the M77 versus ICIT reading disagreements for the same objects: where the two corpora disagree, does an image model side with one? (It gives a third witness on contested sign readings, which affect every statistic.)

entries.title: Indus and Tibetan-Yi Corridor scripts compared by hybrid vision embeddings (ivc2tyc)
entries.question: An image-AI comparison claims Tibetan-Yi corridor scripts resemble Indus signs most.
entries.tried: The author compared sign images from the Indus script, proto-cuneiform and proto-Elamite with signs from newer Dongba, old Naxi and a mixed Tibetan-Yi corridor set of Ba-Shu, Classical Yi and old Naxi signs (section 3.1).
entries.method_data: She trained contrastive CNN-Swin image encoders with an NT-Xent loss at temperature 0.1 (section 3.5). For each target script she trained five models, fifteen in all, each in its own embedding space (section 3.4, Table 3.1). She compared glyph-level and script-level cosine similarity between the target scripts and the corridor set.
entries.key_results: Mean glyph-level cosine similarity with the corridor set is 0.635 for Indus, 0.102 for proto-cuneiform and 0.078 for proto-Elamite (Table 4.1, p. 31). Script-level similarity is 0.930 for Indus (interval 0.917 to 0.942), 0.887 for proto-cuneiform and 0.855 for proto-Elamite (section 4.1.1). Effect sizes (Cohen's d) are 7.13 to 8.36, which the author says are inflated by low variance (Table 4.3; section 5.1.1). Several ensemble members stopped at epoch 1, and validation losses lie roughly between 8.7 and 10.2 (Table 3.1, pp. 23-24). The author lists independent origin, common ancestry and convergent evolution as alternative explanations (section 5.4).
entries.limits: The code is public (github.com/oohalakkadi/ivc2tyc, section 6.3) and the author is open about inflated effect sizes. Similarities from separate embedding spaces, trained per target script, cannot be compared across target scripts. Several models barely trained, so the embeddings may reflect image style more than sign form. Our own red-team run found the Indus advantage disappears when the Ba-Shu signs are removed (experiments/redteam_ivc2tyc).
entries.ideas_for_us: We red-teamed it. The claim technically survives, but its whole edge comes from one small script, Ba-Shu. Proto-cuneiform is closer to Indus than four of the five Himalayan scripts. Retrain one shared embedding space on all scripts together, then compare Indus-to-corridor similarity against a null of shuffled script labels and against unrelated control scripts drawn in a similar style. (This removes the cross-space comparison that makes the published numbers incomparable.) Report the corridor similarity sign by sign and check whether the Indus advantage comes from a handful of simple shapes such as strokes, circles and crosses. (Simple geometric signs recur in unrelated scripts and could drive the result alone.)

entries.title: Origin of the Harappan Ernestites: geochemical insights into provenance and fabrication (with 2026 comment and reply)
entries.authors: Mahala MK, Ray JS, Kanungo AK, et al.; comment Khaliq A; reply Mahala et al.
entries.venue: npj Heritage Science 13:615 (comment and reply Jul 2026)
entries.question: What is Ernestite, the stone used for Harappan long drill bits for beads, and where did it come from?
entries.tried: Mineralogy and Sr-Nd isotopes of Ernestite stones and drill bits from Gujarat sites (e.g. Dholavira, Bhagatrav, Kanmer).
entries.method_data: Petrography, mineral chemistry, 87Sr/86Sr and eNd(0) on stones and drill bits.
entries.key_results: Drill-bit and stone isotopes overlap. A July 2026 comment (Khaliq) disputes the mullite terminology, the ~1100 C estimate (mullite needs >1200 C) and provenance from six samples; the authors' reply upholds their conclusions.

entries.ideas_for_us: Bead-drill technology is a craft marker; Ernestite drills found at sites can be a site covariate (craft-production centre) when testing whether seal sign use differs at manufacturing sites.

entries.title: ALICE: An Interpretable Neural Architecture for Generalization in Substitution Ciphers
entries.question: Can a small transformer learn to solve substitution cryptograms and generalise to unseen keys?
entries.tried: Encoder-only transformer with a bijective Gumbel-Sinkhorn decoding head, trained on English cryptograms.
entries.method_data: Synthetic English cryptograms; probing and early-exit analysis.
entries.key_results: Generalises to unseen ciphers after training on about 1,500 unique ciphers, a 3.7e-24 fraction of the key space. Early layers lean on letter frequency, later layers on word structure.

entries.ideas_for_us: A trained amortised solver is a different attacker class. Training on language A and testing on related language B would be a cheap extra attacker-invariance check.
